samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**An Atlas of Ordinary Places**

I wake before the alarm, which is a habit I acquired without intending to acquire it, somewhere between turning thirty and turning forty, when the body begins to negotiate its own terms. The apartment is still dark except for the thin seam of light under the neighbor's door, and the refrigerator hums its low, indifferent note, and I stand at the kitchen window with a mug that is too hot to drink and watch the street perform its early rehearsals. A cat crosses a fence. A delivery truck idles, exhaling. Somewhere a faucet drips in a rhythm that has not changed in three years. I do not check my phone. I let the day assemble itself in pieces, unhurried, and I think, as I often think at this hour, that I have spent most of my life trying to escape ordinary places, and most of my life failing, and that the failing has been the better part.

When I was seventeen I wanted to leave, not in the vague way that all seventeen-year-olds want to leave, but with a specific, almost cartographic desire. I drew maps in the margins of my notebooks. Not maps of real places, though I copied coastlines from atlases left open in the library, but maps of imagined ones, with rivers that ran uphill and towns connected by roads that no one had yet built. I gave them names that sounded important: Vesper, Hollis, the Lowlands of Marrow. I believed that geography was a kind of destiny, that if I could only arrive at the right coordinate, the rest of my life would arrange itself around that arrival like iron filings around a magnet. I did not understand then that I was already living inside a map, that the cracked sidewalk outside my parents' house, the corner store with its bell, the telephone pole where the flyers for lost dogs accumulated, were already coordinates, already a destiny, just not one I had chosen.

The kitchen table in my childhood home was not a particularly fine table. It was Formica, the color of weak tea, with a metal rim that had been dented by a dropped pressure cooker in 1987, a year I was too young to remember but whose consequences I lived with daily. My mother would attempt to repair the dent with a spoon, pressing and pressing, and my father would tell her to leave it, that it gave the table character. Around that table we did everything that mattered, which is another way of saying we did nothing that would ever be recorded. We ate, we argued about small things, we did not argue about large things because large things were not discussed at that table, or at any table in that house. We did homework there, we played cards there, we sat with the phone cord stretched around a corner so we could have a private conversation in public. The table held all of it without comment, its surface faintly scarred, its edges worn where our arms rested year after year. I have sat at a thousand nicer tables since then, in restaurants with white cloths and in offices with glass tops, and I have never felt as located as I did at that dented table, where the light fell at four o'clock in the afternoon in a particular, slanting way that I can still see if I close my eyes.

There is a library two blocks from where I live now, a brick building that was built in 1934 and has survived every attempt to close it. The librarians there have changed, the carpet has changed, the computers have multiplied like rabbits, but the smell has not changed: paper and dust and the faint, metallic smell of the radiators in winter. I go there not always to read, though I do read, but to be in a place where everyone is engaged in the same quiet, private act. An old man in a windbreaker is grading his granddaughter's spelling test at a table near the window. A teenager is asleep with his head on a copy of *Moby-Dick*, open to a page he will never read. A woman is copying recipes into a notebook in careful handwriting, as if the internet could not be trusted with her mother's soup. The library does not ask anything of us except that we lowball our voices and return what we borrow in roughly the condition we found it. It is a democracy of attention. I have tried to explain this to people who think libraries are obsolete, and I have failed, because what I am describing is not really about books. It is about a place that agrees, on principle, that your inner life is worthwhile, that it deserves a table and a chair and a little bit of light.

I think often about the bus stop on Fifth, which I passed every weekday for six years. It was not a dignified bus stop. There was no shelter, only a sign and a bench that was always damp, and a tree that dropped sap onto the pavement in summer. In winter the wind funneled down Fifth in a way that made waiting feel like a form of penance. And yet that bench became, by accident, a place of extraordinary sociability. I learned the names, or at least the outlines, of the people who waited there: the woman who always wore two different socks, seemingly by design; the man who read *The Racing Form* as if it were scripture; the high school boy who practiced his trumpet scales under his breath, producing notes that sounded like questions. We did not exchange confidences. We exchanged weather commentary and complaints about the bus being late, which it nearly always was, and the occasional, startling piece of news offered without preamble. "My wife left me," the man with the newspaper said one morning, as if reporting rain. "I got into the program," the trumpet boy said another morning, and we all congratulated him with a fervor that surprised us. When I stopped taking that bus, when I moved across town, I missed that bench more than I expected to miss many more luminous things. Ordinary places accumulate a kind of emotional silt. You do not notice it until you walk elsewhere and find your shoes strangely clean.

The river that runs through this city is not a great river. It is the color of machinery and it carries everything the city would prefer to forget: shopping carts, traffic cones, the occasional canoe that has broken free from its mooring and travels like an emissary from another world. In spring it swells and threatens the low houses along its banks, and every few years it does what rivers do, and people stand on their porches and watch their living rooms become aquariums. I walked along it last October, on a morning when the fog had not yet burned off, and I saw a heron standing perfectly still in water that barely covered its ankles. It did not move for a long time. I stood and watched it, and behind me a jogger passed, and ahead of me an old couple walked a dog that was three times their age in dog years and moving with great dignity. The river did not seem to care about any of us. This was not a rejection. It was a relief. There is something honest about a river's indifference. It does not perform for you. It does not ask you to be better. It simply continues, carrying the past downstream without comment, and if you walk beside it long enough, you begin to understand that your own continuity is not so different. You carry things, you forget things, you flood occasionally, and then you recede, and life resumes on the banks, slightly altered, with mud in places where mud was not before.

My grandfather had a workshop in his garage that he was not supposed to use after his heart surgery, and so he used it anyway, with a secrecy that fooled no one. It smelled of sawdust and oil and the faint, sweet smell of pipe tobacco, though he had quit years before. The walls were covered with tools whose names I did not know, hanging on pegboards in outlines he had traced in pencil. There was a radio that was always tuned to the ball game or the weather, depending on the season, and it played to no one in particular, filling the silence with human voices that required no response. I spent afternoons there doing nothing, handing him nails, watching him coax a warped piece of wood into submission. He made things that no one needed: a small stool with three legs, a box for holding screws, a birdhouse that leaned slightly to the left. He would not have called them projects. Projects imply an end. These were simply ways of spending time with his hands. After he died, my father and I cleaned out the workshop, and I found a coffee can full of bent nails that he had straightened rather than thrown away. I still have that can. I do not straighten nails. I am not that kind of person. But I keep the can on a shelf, and when I look at it I remember that usefulness is not the only form of value, and that a life can be measured not by what it produced but by the care with which it was tended.

There is a post office on Main Street that will close next year, according to the notice taped to the window, yellowed already though it has only been up for a month. The clerks there have been there for decades; they know me by sight and, I suspect, by the weight of my packages. The one with the scar on his thumb remembers when the building was a Piggly Wiggly, remembers the flood of '93, remembers when a stamp cost twenty-nine cents and people complained anyway. When I go in to mail something, I stand in line behind someone sending a box to a grandson in Oregon, or someone buying stamps with a coin purse that requires both hands to open. The line moves slowly, ritualistically. It is one of the last places in town where you must interact with a human being to complete a transaction that could be done in three taps on a screen. I do not romanticize this. The line can be infuriating. But there is a kind of civility required in a line, a tacit agreement to be patient with each other's slowness, and I wonder what will replace it when the doors close. Perhaps nothing needs to replace it. Perhaps its closure is simply the next chapter, and the building will become a coffee shop or a vape shop or a memorial to itself. Still, I find myself mailing things there that I could mail elsewhere, just to put my hand on the counter one more time, just to hear the stamp cancelled with that satisfying thump.

I went back to my high school last year for a reunion I did not want to attend and attended anyway. The building had been renovated, of course. The lockers were gone, replaced by glass walls that allowed administrators to see everything, which seemed like an accurate metaphor for adolescence. The courtyard where we used to smoke, though none of us were smokers, had been turned into a rain garden. The gym smelled the same, a mixture of rubber and sweat and cleaning fluid, and for a moment I was sixteen again, sitting on the bleachers, watching a game I did not care about, feeling the peculiar misery of being surrounded by people and feeling utterly alone in a way that only teenagers can master. I found the classroom where I had spent a year learning to fail at algebra, and the teacher, now retired, was there, looking both older and somehow unchanged. "You were bright," she said, "but you were always in a hurry to be somewhere else." She was right, of course. I had been in a hurry to be somewhere else for four years, and then I had been in a hurry to be somewhere else for twenty more, and it was only in the rain garden, listening to the rain fall on leaves that had not been there when I was a student, that I understood how much of that hurry was just a refusal to be where I was.

The train station in the next town over is the kind of place that exists in its own weather. It is an old station, built when trains were a matter of civic pride, with high ceilings and wooden benches and a departure board that clicks and whirs before it changes. No one with any sense of urgency uses that station now; the high-speed line bypasses it, and the parking lot is mostly empty except for a few cars that belong to people who work at the diner across the street. But in the early morning, when the mist is still low, the station is beautiful in a way that has nothing to do with efficiency. Light comes through the tall windows and falls in bars across the floor. A woman sits on a bench with a suitcase at her feet, watching the door as if someone might arrive. A man in a conductor's uniform drinks coffee from a thermos and reads a paperback with a cracked spine. The station does not promise to take you anywhere quickly. It promises only that you will be somewhere, briefly, between where you were and where you are going, and that this betweenness is itself a kind of place, worthy of a bench, worthy of a window, worthy of being built with brick and mortar rather than left to the imagination.

I have a friend who lives in the hills outside town, in a house that is not on any delivery map and that you can only find if you are willing to be lost for a while. The road to her house is gravel and unmarked, and in winter it disappears under snow, and in summer it is lined with wildflowers that look accidental and are not. Her house has a porch that faces west, and from that porch you can see for miles, which is a strange thing to say about a house that is surrounded by trees. But the trees are low, and the hills fall away, and at night the sky is so full of stars that it seems indecent, as if the universe were showing off. She grows tomatoes that she gives away, and she keeps bees that she complains about, and she has a dog that is afraid of thunder and a cat that is afraid of the dog. I go there to do nothing, which in my life has become a discipline rather than a default. We sit on the porch. We watch the light change. We talk about things that do not require resolution. The hills do not care if I am productive. The porch does not care if I am interesting. It is a place that asks less of me than almost any other place I know, and for that reason I leave it feeling more myself than when I arrived.

There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes with knowing a place well. When you know a place well, you know which corners are cold, which lights flicker, which sidewalks are broken in a way that will catch your toe if you are not paying attention. You know the exact spot where the sun hits your windshield at 8:17 in the morning and blinds you for three seconds, and you know to shade your eyes. You know the bakery that is closed on Mondays and the laundromat that smells faintly of bleach even when it is empty. This knowledge is a kind of intimacy, and intimacy, as anyone who has been loved will tell you, is both a comfort and a risk. To know a place well is to be vulnerable to its changes. When the bakery closes for good, when the laundromat becomes a juice bar, when the sidewalk is repaired and no longer broken in that familiar way, you feel a small, irrational grief, as if a friend has altered his personality without consulting you. I have learned to hold my knowledge of places lightly, to expect that they will change, to find new corners to be cold. It is not easy. The heart is a stubborn cartographer. It wants to fix things. It wants to say: here, this is where it was, this is how it was. But places, like people, refuse to be fixed. They insist on continuing.

I keep a drawer of unsent letters. Not letters I intend to send, exactly, but letters I have written at various times in my life to various people, some of whom are still alive and some of whom are not, and all of whom would be surprised, or perhaps not surprised, to receive them now. There is a letter to my father, written when I was twenty-two and angry in a way I can no longer summon, full of accusations that now seem both unfair and beside the point. There is a letter to a woman I loved briefly and intensely at twenty-eight, in which I attempt to explain why I cannot love her in the way she deserves, which is another way of saying I was afraid. There is a letter to myself, written at thirty-five, on a night when I could not sleep, in which I try to be kind to a person who was doing his best under difficult circumstances. I do not send these letters. I do not need to. They serve a purpose in the drawer. They remind me that I have been, at various times, angry, afraid, and kind, and that all three were true, and that the truth of a person is not a single note but a chord, sometimes dissonant, sometimes resolving. The drawer is not a place of shame. It is an archive. I open it occasionally, not to revise, but to remember that I once thought I could explain myself if I just found the right words, and that the right words, when they came, were never quite enough, and that this was not a failure but a condition.

Weather is the great leveler of ordinary places. It does not matter how grand your building is; the rain will find the leak. It does not matter how humble your house is; the snow will cover it in the same white blanket it covers the mansion on the hill. I have come to respect weather in a way I did not when I was younger and thought it was merely an inconvenience. Weather is the one thing that cannot be simulated, cannot be upgraded, cannot be personalized. You cannot choose your weather. You can only dress for it, or fail to dress for it, and live with the consequences. In the summer, the heat settles over the city like a hand, and the air conditioners cough and wheeze, and everyone moves more slowly, and the ice cream shop on the corner does a business that borders on the fraudulent. In the fall, the light changes, becoming gold and then amber and then thin, and the leaves fall with a sound like paper being shuffled, and I find myself walking more, as if the city were more walkable when it is cooler. In winter, the snow makes the familiar strange, turning the bus stop into a sculpture, turning the river into a road, turning the hill behind my friend's house into a possibility. In spring, everything is mud, and then, suddenly, everything is green, and the ordinary places look almost beautiful, as if they have been forgiven.

Silence is also a kind of place, though it is a place we rarely visit intentionally. I do not mean the silence of a library or a church, which is a performed silence, a silence with rules. I mean the silence of an empty room at 3 a.m., the silence of a car in a parking lot after the engine is turned off, the silence of a phone that has not rung in days. This silence is not empty. It is full of all the sounds that are not being made, all the voices that are not speaking, all the life that is happening elsewhere. I used to fear this silence. I would turn on music, turn on the television, turn on something, anything, to fill it. Now I sit in it sometimes, and I find that it is not hostile. It is simply waiting. It is the pause between notes that makes the music possible, and I have learned, slowly, to hear it that way. A place, after all, is not only its sounds. It is also the spaces between them, the quiet blocks where nothing happens and everything that matters is happening anyway, inside a person, inside a memory, inside the slow turning of the earth.

When I was a child, I believed that I would become extraordinary by going to an extraordinary place. I would live in a city with tall buildings, I would work in a job with a title that required a business card, I would be known by people I had not yet met. I did not become extraordinary in that way. I became ordinary in a way that I did not anticipate but that I have come to value more than I can say. I have learned the names of the trees on my street. I have learned which bakery makes the best rye. I have learned that the woman at the post office has a grandson in Oregon and that the man at the bus stop, who is long gone now, had a wife who left him and that he went on, as people do, to have a life that included both grief and, eventually, something like peace. I have learned that extraordinary things happen in ordinary places, not in spite of their ordinariness but because of it. A birth happens in a hospital room that smells of antiseptic. A death happens in a bedroom with a quilt that was made by a grandmother. A love begins on a bus bench that is damp. A life is changed by a sentence spoken in a kitchen with Formica counters. The extraordinary is not elsewhere. It is here, disguised as the ordinary, waiting for us to pay attention.

I am writing this at my kitchen table, which is not Formica but wood, and which I bought secondhand from a man who was moving to a smaller apartment and who told me the table had been his mother's. It has a scratch on one leg where a drawer was kicked open too forcefully, and it wobbles slightly unless I place a folded newspaper under the shorter leg. The light falls on it at four o'clock in the afternoon in a slanting way that reminds me of another table, another kitchen, another version of myself, sitting with a pencil, drawing maps of places that did not exist. I do not know if I have arrived at the right coordinate. I suspect that coordinates are less important than I once thought. I suspect that what matters is not where you are on the map but how you inhabit the place where you are, whether you notice the light, whether you learn the names, whether you leave the bench damp or dry for the next person. The atlas I am making now is not of coastlines or capitals. It is of bus stops and libraries and workshops and porches, of tables that wobble and rivers that do not care, of all the ordinary places that have held me, briefly and without comment, while I figured out how to be a person in the world. It is an atlas that will never be published, that will never be complete, that will be revised every time I walk down a street I thought I knew and find it changed, and every time I sit in silence and hear, not nothing, but everything.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Year I Learned to Look at Trees**

I didn't set out to study trees. I set out to stop being miserable on my commute.

For three years I took the same route to the same office: out my front door, left at the corner shop, down the hill past the bus stop, across the bridge where the river smells of mud in summer and diesel in winter, up the other hill, through a gate in a brick wall that led to a car park, and then a final left into a building with flickering fluorescent lights and a coffee machine that had been broken since 2019. It was a forty-minute walk, or a twenty-two-minute bus ride if I tolerated the patience required to stand while other people did not. I chose the walk most days, not because I loved it, but because it was better than the bus. It was not a beautiful route. It was not a nature walk. It was litter, traffic noise, chain-link fences, and the backs of houses with washing lines strung like tired eyelids.

And in the middle of it, on the corner of Elm Street and something I still cannot name, there was an oak.

I had walked past that oak perhaps eight hundred times before I ever really saw it. It was not the biggest tree I had ever seen. It was not a redwood or a sequoia or one of those ancient village oaks you read about in parish newsletters. It was a street tree, planted probably in the 1970s when the council had a brief enthusiasm for planting. Its trunk was thick enough that I could not wrap my arms around it, its bark was deeply furrowed and grey-brown, and its crown spread wide over the pavement in summer, so that in July I would walk through its shade without thinking. In winter I would walk under its bare branches and think about how cold it was.

One Tuesday in January — I remember it was a Tuesday because the bins had been left out overnight and a fox had scattered chicken bones across the pavement — I stopped under it because my shoelace had come undone. I tied it, standing with my back to the trunk, and I felt, through my coat, the cold and the ridges of the bark. I looked up without any intention. The branches were black against a white sky. A crow was sitting on one, very still, watching me watch it. And I had the absurd, sudden thought: I know nothing about this tree, and this tree has been here longer than I have, and it will be here longer than I will, and I have given it less attention than I give to the adverts on the side of the bus.

So I made a small, private promise, the kind you make when you are sure no one is listening. For one year, I would actually look. Not become a botanist. Not take up arboriculture. Just look, properly, at the trees on my route, and the trees in the park I cut through on weekends, and the trees that showed up in my life in other ways. One year of paying attention.

I didn't keep a notebook at first. I just started noticing names. That is the stupid magic of it: once you learn a name, you cannot unlearn it. For thirty years I had walked around in a world of green blurs. There were trees, and there were other trees. Now suddenly there was an oak, a sycamore with its helicopter seeds in autumn, a lime that smelled impossibly sweet in June, a birch with its papery white bark peeling in strips, a horse chestnut with hands for leaves. I had been, as it turned out, illiterate in my own neighborhood.

### Spring

Spring arrived embarrassingly late that year, or perhaps I arrived embarrassingly late to spring. The first thing I noticed, in March, was not the blossom. Blossom is too obvious, too photogenic; it shouts for attention. The first thing I noticed was the change in the light under the trees in the small park behind the library. The park is not much, just two acres of mown grass, a pond choked with duckweed, a few benches, and a collection of trees planted by people who clearly had no plan but good intentions. In March the ground under the trees was carpeted with snowdrops and then with bluebells, and I realized that I had never connected the two things: the flowers on the ground were there because of the trees above them, because the trees let in light in that brief window before the canopy closed.

A tree leafing out is not a single event. I had always thought of it as a switch: winter bare, spring green. Up close, it is a negotiation. The buds on the oak swelled and split slowly. The lime held out longer. The sycamore seemed to be in a hurry. Some days a tree would look almost green from a distance, and up close you would see that only the outer leaves had opened, pale and curled like fists unclenching. And some mornings I would arrive and a whole branch that had been bare the day before would be suddenly soft with green, as if it had made a decision overnight.

I learned, from a library book I picked up because its cover had no people on it, that a tree is mostly made of air and water and light. That sounded like poetry until I read it twice. A tree's wood is built from carbon pulled out of the air. The sugar it makes in its leaves from sunlight is rearranged into cellulose, into the rigid walls of its cells. So when you touch an old oak, you are touching, in a very literal sense, centuries of captured sunlight and weather. The tree is a solidified history of summers. When I stood under that street oak in May and the air was filled with the green smell of new growth and the leaves were making that soft, restless noise like distant rain, I was standing under a kind of storage battery for the sun.

May brought the blossom I had missed for years because I was looking at my phone while walking. The horse chestnut on the school boundary put out its candles, white and pink and impossibly elaborate, like a chandelier someone had hung in a tree for a party. The hawthorn — I finally learned its name after always calling it the thorny one by the church — flowered and the whole lane smelled suddenly sweet and a little wild, like a hedge that had decided to get married. A blackbird built a nest in the crook of a branch I could see from the pavement, and for two weeks I checked on it every morning like an anxious aunt. I never saw the eggs, but I saw the mother coming and going, and then one morning the fledglings were gone and the nest was empty and the world had moved on without asking my permission. That was a lesson too: to look at a tree is not to possess it. You are a guest.

### Summer

Summer is when trees are easiest to be lazy about. They are at their most themselves, at their fullest, and so you can mistake abundance for simplicity. It took the heat of July to teach me otherwise.

In July the lime trees in the park began to drop their flowers, and the air under them was thick with a perfume so strong it almost made me dizzy. Bees were working in a low, constant hum, and for a while I just stood there, not going anywhere, listening to the sound of a tree being useful to hundreds of other lives. I had thought of trees as scenery, as the green background to human action. That summer I began to think of them as cities. A single mature oak, the library book told me, can support more than two thousand species of insects, birds, fungi, and mammals. Two thousand. On my commute. While I was thinking about whether I needed milk.

I started to see the layers. In the crown, the birds. In the bark, the beetles and the lichens painting it in pale greens and oranges. At the base, the fungi pushing up after rain, some of them poisonous, some of them edible, all of them connected to something I could not see. Underground. The book I was reading kept returning to this: that what we call a tree is only the visible tenth of the organism. The rest is a vast, shallow web of fine roots, and threaded through those roots, the mycelium of fungi, trading nutrients, sending chemical messages, helping one tree feed another in a hard winter. I had spent my life thinking of trees as individuals, lonely and rooted and stoic. The truth, as far as anyone can tell, is almost the opposite. They are social. They are networked. They are, in the words of one scientist I read, more like a forest than like a tree.

I began to wonder what other kinds of loneliness I had mistaken for independence. That is not a scientific thought. Trees do not teach lessons in that tidy way. But standing in a park at noon in August, watching the light move through leaves that had been making sugars all morning, I felt less separate from the place I lived in than I had in years. Not because I had become a nature person. I still hate midges. I still get wet when it rains. But because attention is a form of belonging. You belong to what you pay attention to.

In August, we had a week of extreme heat. The pavement warped a little near the bridge. The river dropped low. The trees, I noticed, suffered differently. The street oak, with its deep roots and its history of summers, seemed unperturbed. The young birch by the bus stop, planted two years earlier, drooped. Its leaves curled inward to conserve water. I found myself, absurdly, worried about it. I carried a bottle of water and poured some at its base on my way home, feeling both foolish and completely serious. A man in a suit, watering a council tree. The tree did not thank me. It did not need to. The soil darkened. That was enough.

### Autumn

Autumn is the season when trees stop pretending to be background and become the main event. In October, my whole route was on fire. The sycamores turned yellow and gold. The oaks went a stubborn, russet brown. The maples — there were only two, but they were showoffs — went scarlet. I had always thought of autumn color as decoration, as something trees did for us. It is not for us. It is a withdrawal. The chlorophyll that made the leaves green and made the sugars all summer is broken down and reabsorbed into the trunk for winter. The colors we see are the pigments that were there all along, masked by green. Autumn is a tree taking back its resources, preparing to let go.

The word "leaf" is a small, inadequate word for what a leaf does. A tree, in autumn, does not just drop leaves. It seals off the base of each leaf with a layer of cells, so that when the leaf falls, the tree does not bleed. It is an amputation performed with care. I watched the street oak negotiate its losses through November. Some leaves turned and fell in a week. Others clung on into December, brown and papery and rattling in the wind. Biologists call them marcescent leaves. I called them stubborn. They were the last of summer, refusing to leave.

My mother, who had always been a gardener of the relentless, optimistic sort, used to sweep leaves from our driveway in November with a kind of fury, as if the tree were being rude. That autumn, she was ill. Not catastrophically, but enough to keep her mostly indoors, looking out of the window at the ash tree in her garden while her mobility faded a little more each week. I visited on Sundays and we would sit and watch the leaves fall, or rather, she would watch and I would try to be patient. She told me that when she was a girl, during the war, her school had taken them to count rings on a felled tree to learn how old it was. She remembered being disappointed that it wasn't as old as they had hoped. She wanted it to be ancient. I told her about dendrochronology, about how scientists can read a tree's life in its rings: wide rings for wet years, narrow for dry, a frost ring for the year of the great freeze. She liked that. She said trees kept diaries, but in wood.

I thought about that for days afterwards. My mother kept a diary in a small red book, in pencil, for forty years. I have read only a few pages since she died, and only by accident. Trees keep their diaries in the open. Anyone with a saw and a willingness to cut could read them. But we walk past them every day without reading a word.

In November, the council cut back the trees along the river path. They do it each year, a brutal, efficient pollarding. I was annoyed on their behalf. Branches that I had watched all year, that held the blackbird's nest, that cast the shade I had relied on, were hacked back to stumps. It looked violent. And then I learned that many of these trees had been pollarded for centuries, that it is a traditional way of managing them, that the wood they produce is straight and useful, and that the tree, in its patience, would grow again. I needed to learn that the tree's relationship to cutting is different from mine. The tree does not experience it as an ending. It experiences it as a season. I am still learning how to think like that.

### Winter

Winter is when you learn whether you really mean it about paying attention. In winter, there is nothing to hide behind. No blossom, no green, no color. There is only structure. There is only the architecture of a tree, laid bare.

In January, I stood under the street oak again, a year after the shoelace. The sky was the same white. The crow was gone, or it was a different crow. The branches were black and intricate and, I could now see, full of life. The buds were tight and closed, waiting. In the crook of a branch, a mistletoe ball clung, green against the grey. Higher up, a squirrel's drey, a messy ball of twigs. Down the trunk, ivy made its dark green climbs. The tree in winter is not empty. It is resting. It is holding its breath so it can survive.

A friend of mine, after I had been talking about trees for a few months, said, “You’ve become a tree bore.” He meant it kindly. I took it as a compliment. Because there is a kind of boredom that is a form of attention. To look at the same tree every day for a year is, for most people, to look at the same thing. To look at the same tree every day for a year is also to see that it is never the same. The light changes. The weather changes. The tree changes. You change. After a while, the sameness becomes the point. You learn the tree the way you learn a neighbor's face: not all at once, but in the accumulation of small, unremarkable encounters.

I have a theory, which I would not defend in a scientific paper but which feels true to me, that we are all, to some extent, pollarded by life. We get cut back. We lose leaves. We lose whole branches. We go through winters where we look bare and architecture-like and dead to anyone passing. And in those winters, if anyone is paying attention, they might see that the buds are still there. That the tree is not dead. That it is wait­ing, in the only way a tree can wait: by holding its structure and conserving its sugars and trusting, without any evidence, that the light will return.

Do trees trust? That is anthropomorphism, certainly. But I have stood under that oak in the rain, under the birch in the heat, under the lime when it smelled like heaven, and I have felt something that I can only call companionship. Not friendship. Trees do not know my name. But companionship does not require that. It only requires presence over time.

### What the Trees Taught Me

I do not know the Latin names for half the trees I can now identify. I know the common ones because I asked, and because I am stubborn, and because my phone, which I still carry, can identify a leaf if I hold it up to the camera and apologize to it for doing so. I know that the oak on Elm Street is a pedunculate oak, Quercus robur, which I learned from a man on a bench who turned out to be a retired forester and who was delighted to tell me. I know that the sycamore is not a true maple but an impostor that arrived from Europe and stayed. I know that the lime is a Tilia, sacred to lovers in ancient Greece, which is why it smells the way it does in June.

I also know things that are not in books. I know that the horse chestnut by the school gets its blossom earlier in warm years, and that in 2024 it flowered in late April, and that the children noticed before I did. I know that the blackbirds prefer the hawthorn to the oak. I know that the park's pond, in winter, freezes at the edges first, and that the ducks stand on the ice with one foot up, as if they are testing the world. I know that my mother, who could name every plant in her garden in two languages, never learned the name of the ash tree outside her window until I told her, and that she then called it “Ash” for the rest of her life, as if it were a person. Perhaps it was.

At the end of the year, I walked my route one last time with the intention of saying goodbye. It was a cold, clear December afternoon. The light was low and golden, the kind of light that makes even a car park look briefly noble. The oak stood bare and perfect, its branches etched against the sky. A few brown leaves rattled in the wind. I put my hand on its trunk, just to put my hand on its trunk. It was cold and rough and solid. It did not move. It has never moved, in any way I can understand, and yet it has been in a state of continuous, intricate change for longer than my family has lived in this town.

I had started the year thinking I was going to learn about trees. I ended it realizing that I had learned, instead, how to be in a place. How to be somewhere without being somewhere else. How to walk without earphones so that I could hear the leaves. How to notice the season not by the calendar on my phone, but by the smell of lime blossom, by the fall of sycamore keys, by the first frost on the birch. How to look at something for a long time without needing to own it, or use it, or explain it.

Next year, I will probably forget some of the names. I will probably get busy and walk past the oak without stopping. I will probably check my phone under its shade and miss the crow. That is fine. The tree will not keep score. The tree will be there anyway, making its slow, wooden diary, ring by ring, year by year, reading to anyone who stops long enough to listen.

I untied my shoelace one more time, although it was not undone. I stood there a minute longer than I needed to. And then I walked on, through the branches' shadow, toward the bridge, toward winter, toward whatever came next, walking like a person who had finally learned which street he lived on.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I woke up this morning before the alarm, which is something that rarely happens and therefore felt like a small, private gift intended only for me. The room was still dim, the color of water in a glass left overnight, and for a while I lay there listening to the house settle into itself, the faint ticking of the radiator, the distant rumble of a delivery truck, the soft breath of the building as it warmed. I did not reach for my phone. I did not jump immediately into the list of things waiting for me. I simply watched the light change.

When I finally got up, the kitchen was cold in the particular way kitchens are cold in the early hours, as if the room had been holding its breath all night. I filled the kettle, which is a ritual I have never managed to skip, even when I am in a hurry, even when the day is already pressing against the windows. There is something about the click of the switch, the low roar that begins and grows, that tells my body what time it is more honestly than any clock. While the water heated, I stood with my hands around a chipped mug and looked out at the back fence, at the neighbor's cat moving with great seriousness along the top of it, and I felt, absurdly, grateful to be awake in a world that had not asked anything of me yet.

My grandmother used to say that mornings belonged to the people who made tea properly, which in her house meant waiting until the pot was fully hot and then pouring the water in a high, steady arc so that it struck the leaves and woke them all at once. She would hum while she did it, not a real tune, just a thin thread of sound. I think about her hands often — spotted, strong, always busy — and about how she could make a room feel orderly without ever appearing to tidy. She believed that attention was a form of kindness, that you could love a person or a place simply by noticing it accurately. I did not understand that when I was a child. I thought kindness meant gifts, or apologies, or showing up with flowers. Now I think she might have been right.

Outside, the street had that early quiet that feels different from the quiet of night. It was not empty, exactly. It was full of small beginnings. A man hosed down his front step. A woman carried a bag of recycling to the curb and paused to look at the sky, as if checking on something. Someone’s radio was on low in an open kitchen window, a weather report murmured and then a song I did not know. I walked slowly to the corner shop, not because I needed anything in particular, but because I wanted to be a person in the world for a few minutes before the day hardened into tasks. The air smelled faintly of rain that had fallen hours ago and of bread from the bakery two doors down.

Mrs. Alvarez runs that shop, or perhaps it runs her, and she knows everyone’s usual order in a way that feels almost like memory. She asked about my sister, who lives far away now and writes letters that take two weeks to arrive and then stay on my desk for a month because I like having them there. We talked about the price of eggs and the new paint color on the flats across the street and whether the pigeons had taken over the bus shelter again. None of it mattered, and all of it did. This is the thing I keep coming back to: that a life is not made of one great sweeping purpose, but of hundreds of small, repeatable exchanges in which people briefly agree to be gentle with each other.

On the way home, I passed the school and watched children spill out in bright, noisy waves, their backpacks larger than their torsos, their arguments already ancient and serious. A boy was trying to teach another boy a magic trick with a coin, and both of them were completely absorbed, moving their hands back and forth, laughing at the failure and the success in equal measure. I stood still for a moment, not wanting to interrupt, and I thought about how much of adult life is about pretending we still know the trick, about holding our hands out confidently and hoping no one asks to see them close up. The children did not care about looking foolish. They cared about the coin disappearing. I envied them that clarity.

Later, at my desk, the phone lit up and lit up again, a small constellation of demands. Messages, headlines, photographs of other people’s lunches, invitations, reminders, a video of a dog learning to skateboard. Each one arrived with its own small urgency, as if the world would collapse if I did not look at it within the next thirty seconds. I put the phone in another room, which is a dramatic gesture I perform perhaps twice a week, and I sat with the silence it left behind. The silence was not empty. It was full of the ticking clock, the traffic, the faint ache in my shoulder from sleeping badly, and, underneath all that, my own thoughts unedited. I had forgotten how many of them there were.

Attention, I have come to think, is not a natural talent so much as a muscle that gets tired. We praise people for being focused, as if focus were a moral virtue, but mostly we are just tired, and tired people look at their phones. I do not blame anyone for that. I blame the design, perhaps, and also myself, and also the simple fact that human beings have always been distractible. My grandmother told me that when she was young, people would wait for the evening news to find out what had happened in their own city. Can you imagine the patience that required? She said it like a complaint and like a boast at the same time. I think about that patience now when I am waiting for water to boil or for a web page to load, and I try to borrow a little of it.

There is a tree on my street that no one planted on purpose, or perhaps someone did and then forgot, and it has grown crooked in the space between two brick walls. Its roots have lifted the pavement in soft, regular bumps, like the knuckles of a hand. In spring it throws green light onto the windows opposite. In autumn it drops leaves that collect in corners and make a dry, rustling music when the wind finds them. I have watched that tree through four seasons without ever thinking I was “watching a tree.” It was just there, interrupting my walk, shading my head, getting in the way of my bicycle. And yet, if it were cut down tomorrow, I would notice the absence every single time I passed, and I would feel a small, irrational grief, as if a minor character had been removed from a book I was reading.

My work, when it is good, involves my hands. I do not mean art, exactly, though sometimes it could be called that. I mean the simple, repetitive tasks that let my mind wander while my body stays busy: folding laundry until the edges align, sanding a piece of wood until it feels smooth enough to trust, typing and retyping a sentence until it sounds like something a person might actually say. There is a particular pleasure in work that leaves a visible trace, in arranging and rearranging until a pile becomes a shelf, a draft becomes a page, a messy drawer becomes a place where things can be found. Digital work vanishes when you close the laptop. Hand work remains. It sits there, slightly imperfect, and says: someone was here, and they cared enough to try.

I have been rereading a novel I first read at nineteen, and I am struck by how different it is now, not because the words have changed but because I have. Then, I underlined everything. I wrote in the margins, in a handwriting I no longer recognize, about fate and beauty and whether the ending was sad. Now I find myself underlining almost nothing and noticing details I missed entirely: the way the author describes a character’s coat, the repeated image of a train window, the small moment of kindness in chapter three that I had completely forgotten. Rereading feels like revisiting a house you once lived in and finding that the light falls differently at different times of your life. The house has not moved. You have.

Music has a way of bypassing all my careful explanations. I can be in the middle of a perfectly reasonable thought — about money, about plans, about whether I should call someone back — and a song will start somewhere, on a passing car radio or in a café, and suddenly I am thirteen again, or twenty-two, or standing in a kitchen in a city I no longer live in, holding a glass of water and trying not to cry and failing. I do not think this is nostalgia, exactly, though nostalgia is part of it. I think it is the brain’s filing system, tagging moments with sound for easy retrieval. The song is a key. The door opens. I step through, and for a second I am both who I was and who I am, and neither version is entirely true, and both are.

My friend Tomas and I have a standing appointment to get coffee on Thursdays, which we do not always keep, but the intention matters. When we do meet, we sit at the same table by the window and talk about everything except the things we are supposed to talk about. We discuss our neighbors’ dogs, the correct way to make a soup, the strange dreams we have had, the book Tomas is pretending to read. Sometimes we talk about serious things — his father’s health, my job, the fear that we are slowly becoming less interesting to the world — but we approach those subjects sideways, as one might approach a shy animal, with food and patience. I think friendship in adulthood is largely the art of agreeing to keep showing up, even when the conversation is only about soup. Especially when the conversation is only about soup.

Cooking is another place where I like to be slow. Not fancy cooking, not the kind that requires equipment I do not own and ingredients I cannot pronounce. I mean the kind where you put onions and garlic in oil and watch them turn translucent, where you add carrots and celery and let them soften, where you pour in stock and watch the pot begin to breathe. It takes an hour, sometimes two, and during that hour the whole apartment changes. The air becomes warm and seasoned. The windows fog slightly. I find myself tasting and adjusting, adding a pinch of salt, a squeeze of lemon, a handful of herbs I have no real plan for. It is a deeply undemanding form of creativity, and it feeds people, which is more than can be said for most creative pursuits.

I am getting older, which is to say that time is getting faster, or at least my perception of it is. When I was a child, summer lasted forever. It had its own geography, its own boredom, its own endless afternoons when the light seemed to refuse to leave. Now, a week can disappear in a blink, and I will have nothing to show for it except a vague sense of having been busy. I have started keeping a small notebook by my bed, not a journal, exactly, but a list of things that happened that I do not want to forget: the exact shade of the sky on Tuesday, the joke my neighbor told, the song in the shop. It is a clumsy defense against forgetfulness. It does not work very well. But writing it down, however briefly, seems to slow the day down just a fraction, as if the act of noticing is itself a kind of preservation.

There is a particular dignity in mending things instead of replacing them, and I have become more interested in that dignity as I have gotten older and, frankly, poorer. I mend shirts. I tighten the handle on a pan that has been in my family for longer than I have been alive. I glue a mug that was a gift and that I refused, on principle, to throw away. The repairs are visible. You can see the thread, the seam, the slight wobble where the glue set. I like that visibility. It tells a story. A world in which everything is new and seamless and disposable is a world that asks us to forget that things break, that people break, that repair is not failure but a second chance offered with a needle and thread. My grandmother darned socks. She was not being thrifty, though she was that too. She was being honest.

Rain arrived in the afternoon, sudden and theatrical, drumming on the awning outside the café and turning the street into a mirror. People ran for doorways, holding newspapers over their heads in the old-fashioned way, as if the year were 1975 and newspapers still provided adequate shelter. I stayed a little longer than necessary, watching the drops make expanding circles in the puddles, listening to the abrupt change in the city’s soundscape. Rain has a way of making the world feel briefly new, as if it has been washed and set down again, slightly damp and brighter. I thought about how many times I have wished for rain to clear the air, and how rarely I have wished for anything else in quite so uncomplicated a way. Sometimes the simplest desires are the most reliable.

At night, when the rain has stopped and the air is clean, I sometimes stand on the balcony and look up. The stars are not as bright here as they were where I grew up, where the sky was so dark you could see the pale smudge of the Milky Way like a river of spilled milk. Here, the light from the city thins them out, and you have to search for them, a few stubborn points among the orange haze. I have learned to find Orion by first finding the brightest thing and then moving sideways, a small act of navigation that feels like a trick I am playing on myself. It does not matter that I cannot see very many. I like knowing they are there, indifferent and ancient, while I stand in my slippers with a cup of tea going cold in my hand.

Dreams have been vivid lately, the kind that leave you disoriented for an hour after waking, unsure whether you have already had the conversation you are about to have. In one, I was late for a train that was also a house I had lived in as a child, and I kept going up and down stairs that led to rooms I recognized and did not recognize. In another, I was trying to explain to a stranger why I had arrived without shoes, and the stranger understood perfectly, which felt like a rebuke. I do not believe dreams are messages, exactly, though I understand why people want them to be. I think they are the mind sorting through its attic, throwing things around, occasionally finding something useful, occasionally making a mess. Still, I keep a glass of water by the bed, out of habit, and I try to remember the best parts before they dissolve.

Small pleasures have started to feel less small to me. The first sip of coffee. The way sunlight falls across a wooden table at four in the afternoon. A text from someone I love that says nothing in particular. The moment when a difficult paragraph finally yields and becomes two easy ones. The smell of a library, which is paper and dust and quiet. I used to think happiness would arrive in large, unmistakable packages, delivered to the door with a return address. Now I think it arrives more like weather, or like a good neighbor: unannounced, ordinary, and easy to overlook if you are waiting for something grander. I am trying, imperfectly, to be the kind of person who notices when it is there.

In the evening, after the dishes are done and the apartment has cooled slightly, I like to sit with a book and a blanket and do absolutely nothing that could be considered productive. This is harder than it sounds. My mind wants to rehearse tomorrow, to make lists, to check whether I have replied to that email. I have learned to treat the urge as background noise, like traffic, and to return, gently and repeatedly, to the page in front of me. Sometimes I succeed for twenty minutes, which feels like a triumph. Sometimes I succeed for two. Either way, the book waits. It does not scold me for my wandering. It simply stays open, patient, offering me a sentence I can sink into like a chair.

Seasons are a kind of syllabus for attention. Spring teaches you to watch for beginnings, to notice buds and first blossoms and the sudden confidence of birds. Summer teaches you to endure heat and light and the long, slow afternoons when nothing seems to happen. Autumn teaches you to let go, to watch color change and leaves fall and accept that some things are beautiful precisely because they are leaving. Winter teaches you to be still, to keep the kettle going, to find warmth in small, deliberate acts. I have lived in this neighborhood for long enough to see the same trees perform this curriculum four times, and I have not yet learned it by heart. Each year, I am surprised by something: the first snow, the last leaf, the day when the light suddenly seems different and I realize, with a little shock, that I have crossed into another season without noticing.

Silence used to frighten me. I filled it with music, with podcasts, with the low murmur of television, with anything that would keep me from hearing my own thoughts too clearly. I think many of us do that, especially now, when silence is so easy to banish with a tap. But I have been spending more time in silence lately, not as a discipline, not as a performance of mindfulness, but simply because I am tired of noise. I walk without headphones. I sit without a screen. I let a moment stretch. The silence is not empty. It is full of the world moving at its own pace, and I am, for once, moving at roughly the same pace, not trying to outrun it, not trying to optimize it, just being there while it happens.

When I was a child, my favorite game was to pretend that the world had a secret level, accessible only if you knew the right way to look at it. I would stare at a wall until the pattern of the wallpaper seemed to shift, or I would hold a bottle cap up to my eye and imagine I could see through the other side of the planet. I do not play that game anymore, but I understand now that it was not childish. It was a way of practicing wonder. Adults do it too, when they are at their best: they look at ordinary things until they reveal a second layer. A conversation reveals a history. A street reveals a neighborhood. A person you have known for years reveals, on an ordinary Thursday over coffee, a worry they have never voiced before. The secret level is still there. You just have to learn how to look.

Language is a slippery thing, and I am often aware of how poorly it serves the things I most want to say. I can describe a soup in exhaustive detail, but I cannot quite describe what it feels like to miss someone who is still alive and living a perfectly ordinary life three time zones away. I can say “I am fine” when I am not, and “I am sorry” when I do not entirely know what I am sorry for, and “see you soon” when soon is a vague and unreliable country. Still, I keep trying. I write letters. I send messages that are too long. I say the clumsy, true thing instead of the smooth, false thing, and I accept that I will sometimes be misunderstood. That is the price of speaking. The alternative — silence, perfect and unexposed — feels too high.

There are days when I feel that I have wasted time, days when the hours have poured through me like water through a sieve, leaving nothing behind. I try not to judge those days too harshly. I remind myself that rest is not waste, that boredom is not failure, that the mind needs fallow periods in which nothing appears to grow. I remember my grandmother’s garden, which she tended with a mixture of care and neglect that seemed to work perfectly: she watered when it needed water, she left it alone when it needed to be left alone, and she never, as far as I could tell, apologized to the soil for taking a day off. Gardens, like people, do not thrive on constant attention. They thrive on attention at the right time, and on being left to do their quiet work in between.

In the end, I suppose the point is not to solve anything. I do not have a thesis, unless the thesis is that a life of noticing — noticing the kettle, the tree, the neighbor, the light, the soup, the stars — is a life worth living, even if it does not add up to a story that can be told at a dinner party. Maybe it adds up to something better: a texture, a grain, a way of being in the world that is kind to itself and to others. I will go to bed tonight, and I will probably wake up before the alarm again, or I will not, and either way the house will settle and the kettle will click and the street will fill with its small beginnings. And I will try, once more, to pay attention, not because it makes me a better person, but because, for reasons I cannot fully explain, it makes the world feel larger, and more forgiving, and more mine.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**What We Keep: A Free Meditation on Memory, Objects, and the Art of Letting Go**

If you open almost any drawer in almost any house in the world, you will find a version of the same small, mysterious archive. There will be a key that no longer fits any lock you own, a screw, a dead battery, a cable for a device you threw away years ago, a ticket stub softened at the edges, a photograph of people you cannot quite name anymore, and a letter you meant to answer and never did. None of these things are useful in any practical sense, and yet we keep them, often for decades, moving them from apartment to apartment, from box to box, as if some quiet instinct told us that to throw them away would be to lose a piece of a story we have not finished telling ourselves. This essay is about that instinct, about why we keep, why we forget, and why the objects we hold on to say more about us than the things we carefully choose to preserve.

We are, all of us, accidental archivists. We do not set out in the morning intending to build a museum of our lives, and most of us would be horrified if someone described us that way. We think of ourselves as practical people who throw things away. And yet, if you look honestly at any inhabited space, you will find layers of preservation that no curator would have planned. A chipped mug from a first apartment because it was a gift. A book with a sentence underlined in pencil from a summer when you thought you understood everything. A coat that no longer fits but that you wore on a night you still think about. These are not decisions. They are accumulations. Memory does not file itself neatly; it clings to surfaces, to smells, to weight and texture, and it drags those things along with it long after the moment that created them has dissolved. We keep because forgetting feels like a second loss.

History, as a discipline, was invented by people who distrusted that kind of clinging. They wanted records that could survive a single lifetime, that could be checked against other records, that would not fade when the owner died or moved house. So they built archives and libraries and museums, vast, climate-controlled rooms where the past was supposed to behave itself. But there is a strange irony in those institutions: they preserve so much more than human memory ever could, and at the same time they preserve it so much worse. A letter in an archive can tell you what a man in 1843 thought about grain prices and his sister's marriage, but it cannot tell you why his handwriting changed in the winter of his grief, or why he kept a pressed flower inside a book that had nothing to do with flowers. The archive gives us the fact. The drawer gives us the feeling. We need both, and we are always dissatisfied with both.

Consider the brain itself, which is perhaps the most dishonest archivist of all. Neurologists will tell you, in polite and complicated language, that memory is not a recording but a reconstruction, rebuilt every time you summon it, slightly different each time, influenced by your mood, your conversation, the question someone asked you five minutes earlier. This sounds like a flaw, and in a courtroom it would be. But in a life, it is a mercy. If we remembered everything with perfect clarity, we would be crushed by the sheer volume of detail: every awkward sentence, every face on a train, every rainy Tuesday in a job we disliked. Forgetting is not a failure of the system. It is the system. It edits. It compresses. It allows a story to emerge from noise. The trouble is that we cannot control the editing. We forget the name of the street where we learned to ride a bicycle, but we remember, twenty years later, the exact sound of a kettle in a kitchen we only visited once. The archive of the mind has no index. It has only association, and association is a capricious librarian.

This is why we outsource memory to objects. A photograph promises to do what the brain will not: to hold a face still while time moves. A notebook promises to hold a thought while the mind wanders. A ticket stub promises proof that we were there, that the journey actually happened, that we were younger and braver or more foolish than we are now. We gather these external memories not because we are sentimental, although some of us are, but because we are aware, at some level, that we are temporary. The objects will outlast the feeling, and perhaps, if we are lucky, the feeling will come back when we touch them again. It is a small, hopeful magic trick: put a dried leaf between the pages of a book, and months later, when you open it, the smell of autumn in another city will rise up and knock you sideways. No database has ever done that as reliably.

Walter Benjamin, who understood nostalgia better than almost anyone, once wrote about the aura of an object — that strange quality it acquires from having existed in a particular time and place, from having been handled by particular hands. A chair that has held four generations of a family is not the same chair, even if it is made of the same wood in the same workshop, as an identical chair that has never left the factory. The difference is invisible and unmeasurable, but we feel it immediately when we sit down. The same is true of a house, a street, a song. We do not keep things because they are rare or valuable. We keep them because they have been somewhere with us. They are witnesses. And we are lonely enough, and curious enough about our own past, that we want witnesses who cannot argue back.

If you doubt that this is a universal human impulse and not a peculiarity of modern, cluttered life, consider how ancient the impulse is. The earliest archaeologists have found, buried with the dead in caves and early villages, not just tools and weapons but shells, polished stones, animal teeth, beads of bone — objects that had no obvious use beyond being beautiful or meaningful or simply *kept*. Someone, tens of thousands of years ago, picked up a strange stone because it pleased them and carried it home and placed it with the person they loved after that person died. That is the same gesture as the modern drawer. The scale is different, the materials are different, but the human intention is identical: this mattered to me, let it stay near me, let it stay near them. Long before we had writing, we had keeping. The first museum was a pocket.

And yet there is a shadow to all this keeping. Anyone who has helped clear out a parent's house after a death knows the double feeling that arrives. First, there is the tenderness: to find a birthday card you made at age seven, saved for fifty years. Then, there is the exhaustion and the ambiguity: why did they keep the broken umbrella? Why are there eleven identical plastic containers with no lids? Why did they save every newspaper from 1998? At some point, keeping stops being memory and starts being weight. Psychologists have names for this, and there are television shows that turn it into entertainment, but the real experience is quieter and sadder. It is the realization that the person we loved was also a person who could not let go, and that their inability to let go was perhaps not about objects at all, but about fear — fear of waste, fear of being forgetful, fear of dying and having nothing to show that they had lived. The archive can become a mausoleum if we are not careful. We start to preserve not because something is meaningful, but because we are afraid that if we throw it away, we will prove that nothing was meaningful.

There is a whole philosophy, now popular and commercially successful, that promises to solve this problem by teaching us to ask of each object, “Does this spark joy?” It is a good question, but it is an incomplete one. Joy is a narrow criterion. Many of the most important objects in a life do not spark joy. They spark grief, or obligation, or confusion, or a dull, steady sense of responsibility. A wedding ring after a divorce does not spark joy. It sparks a complicated history. A letter from a friend who died does not spark joy. It sparks absence. A textbook from a degree you never finished does not spark joy. It sparks a version of yourself that you abandoned. If we only kept what made us happy in the moment, we would edit our lives down to a highlight reel, and highlight reels are lies. Sometimes we need to keep the difficult things precisely because they do not spark joy, because they remind us that a life is not a product to be curated, but a story to be understood.

Perhaps the most honest way to think about keeping is not as accumulation but as conversation. Every object we retain asks us a question: why am I still here? And every time we move house, or clean a closet, or sit down with a box we have avoided for years, we have a chance to answer differently. Sometimes the answer is: because you still teach me something. Sometimes the answer is: because I am not ready to say goodbye to the person who gave you to me. Sometimes the answer, finally, is: I do not know, and I no longer need to justify you. And then, with a strange freedom, we can let it go. Not because we have forgotten, but because we have finally understood what it was trying to tell us, and we no longer need the messenger.

The digital age has complicated this conversation beyond anything our ancestors could have imagined. We now keep more than any generation in history, effortlessly, without the physical burden that once forced us to choose. A phone can hold ten thousand photographs, a lifetime of letters, every song we ever loved, every map we ever followed, in a device smaller than a paperback book. This sounds like a triumph over forgetting, and in some ways it is. A grandmother who once would have lost a photograph in a fire can now share it instantly with grandchildren she will never meet. A researcher who once would have spent months in archives can now search millions of documents in an afternoon. But there is a cost, and it is not only the obvious one about privacy or attention. The cost is that when everything is kept, nothing is chosen, and when nothing is chosen, the act of keeping loses its meaning. A drawer full of mysterious objects is poignant because someone, consciously or not, decided — by a thousand small acts of not throwing away — that those things mattered. A cloud full of images is just storage. It does not ache in the same way.

There is also the paradox of digital memory: it is both more permanent and more fragile than the objects in our drawer. The key in the drawer will work, or not work, in fifty years exactly as it does now. The photograph printed on paper will fade, but it will still be a photograph. The file on a hard drive, however, depends on a chain of technologies that may not exist in fifty years: the right cable, the right software, the right password, the company that still maintains the server. We have moved from keeping things to keeping *access* to things, and access, unlike a stone, can be revoked. The future archaeologist who wants to understand us will not dig through our landfills and find a neat drawer. She will find a data center and try to guess which of our trillion files were the ones we actually cared about. She will have a harder job than we do with our grandparents' junk drawers, where the act of keeping was itself the message.

And so perhaps we should learn, again, the older art: to keep slowly, and to forget deliberately. Not the aggressive forgetting of denial, but the gentle forgetting that allows a memory to settle into the background, where it can do its work without demanding constant attention. Many cultures have rituals for this. The Japanese custom of *mottainai* reminds us that waste is a kind of ingratitude. The Mexican Day of the Dead reminds us that remembering the dead is an active, joyful labor, not a passive ache. The simple practice of writing a letter and then burning it — a tradition in several religions — reminds us that some things are meant to be sent upward, not stored. In each case, the ritual acknowledges that memory is not just accumulation. It is also release. It is a way of saying: I have carried this as far as it can go, and now I will let it carry itself.

I think often about the moment when an object stops being a memory and becomes just an object again. It happens quietly. You come across the coat, and instead of feeling the night you wore it, you feel only its weight and the inconvenience of storing it. You open the book, and the underlined sentence no longer speaks to you. You look at the photograph, and the faces are clear but the emotion is gone, as if someone turned down the volume. This is not betrayal. It is the natural end of an object's career as a witness. It has testified. It has done its work. The temptation is to feel guilty for no longer feeling, to force the emotion back by sheer will. But guilt is a poor archivist. It preserves things in a state of resentment. It is better to thank the object, acknowledge what it held, and allow it to become, again, a coat, a book, a piece of paper. Only then can it be given away, recycled, or returned to the earth without a sense of loss.

If this sounds too philosophical for a junk drawer, that is perhaps the point. The smallest things contain the largest questions. What does it mean to have lived? How will we be remembered, and by whom, and in what form? Is it better to be remembered accurately or to be remembered vividly? These are not questions we can answer once and for all, and we should be suspicious of anyone who claims we can. But we can practice answering them in miniature, every time we decide what to keep and what to release. Each decision is a small vote for the kind of person we want to be: someone who hoards out of fear, someone who discards out of impatience, or someone who keeps with intention and lets go with gratitude.

I have a friend who keeps a small wooden box on his desk. Inside it is not jewelry or letters, but smooth stones he has collected on walks in different countries over the last twenty years. Each stone is unremarkable on its own — gray, brown, speckled, ordinary. He can tell you where each one came from, what kind of day it was, who he was with, what he was thinking about. He has never displayed them. He rarely opens the box. But he told me once that knowing the box exists changes how he walks. He pays attention now. He looks down. He slows his pace to notice the edges of paths and riverbanks. The stones taught him to see. That, I think, is the best argument for keeping: not that it preserves the past, but that it improves the present. A kept object is a prompt to attention. It says: I was here, I noticed this, I thought it was worth carrying. And in that small act of carrying, we become slightly more conscious of the world we are carrying ourselves through.

There will come a time, of course, when we will no longer be here to open the drawer. Someone else — a child, a partner, a stranger hired to clear a house — will stand where we stood, holding the key that fits no lock, wondering what to do with us. This is the final, humbling irony of all our keeping: we will be reduced, for a moment, to what we could not let go of. The boxes we leave behind will be our last, accidental autobiography. We cannot control how that story will be read. The reader may be tender and keep everything. The reader may be practical and throw it all away. The reader may keep one thing — the photograph, the letter, the stone — and that one thing will stand, in their mind, for the whole of a life. This is both terrifying and oddly comforting. It means that the meaning of a life is never finally decided by the person who lived it. It is always co-written, edited, and reinterpreted by those who come after.

Perhaps that is why, in the end, the most meaningful act of keeping is not to keep objects at all, but to keep people in mind with enough care that we can tell their stories well. Objects fade, drawers are emptied, data decays. But a story, told and retold, can survive being misremembered. It can travel from one generation to the next, changing shape as it goes, like a folktale. The grandmother who saved every card may be forgotten, but the story of why she saved them — because she was lonely in a new country, because she wanted her grandchildren to know they were loved before she could say it herself — that story can live. And it can live without a single physical object to prove it. The best archive, in the end, is not a room or a box or a cloud. It is a person who says, “Let me tell you about someone who kept a key for forty years, and this is what it meant.”

So let us return, one last time, to the drawer. Open it. Look inside. Do not judge what you find. Pick up the key. Wonder about the lock you have lost. Pick up the ticket. Remember the journey, even if you cannot remember the destination. Pick up the letter you never answered, and consider, for a moment, whether it is too late to answer it now, in a different way — by writing to someone else, by forgiving yourself, by finally letting the words rest. The drawer is not a problem to be solved. It is a companion to be consulted. It will not tell you who you are. But if you listen carefully, and if you are willing to keep some things and release others, it might help you become who you want to be.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
If I were to be honest, which is a strange thing to promise in advance, I don't have a plan for this. I was given a blank space and a number — 2500 words — and the freedom to do whatever I want inside it, and the first honest feeling that arrived was not inspiration but a mild vertigo. Freedom that complete is disorienting. Most writing has a prompt, a shape to lean against: explain this, argue that, tell a story about a dog. Write *freely* about *whatever* — it's like being told you can go anywhere in an infinite city and then standing still on the sidewalk because every direction is equally possible and therefore paralyzing.

So I will start where I always start when I don't know what to do: with something small and in front of me. On my desk right now is a chipped mug with tea gone cold, a pencil chewed at the end, a notebook that has collected more starts than finishes, and a window that looks out onto a fence and then, beyond the fence, a neighbor's tree. The tree has been there longer than the fence. The light is doing that thing it does in the late afternoon, angling through the leaves and making the wall look warmer than it is. A bird, probably a sparrow, has decided that the top of the fence is a very important post to defend. It comes back. It leaves. It comes back.

I could write about the bird. I could write about tea. I could write about the pencil. The point, or perhaps the absence of a point, is that any of these could swallow the whole assignment if I let them. Free writing is not really free. It just pretends the leash is longer.

Let me try a different tack. Let me think about what I actually *like* to notice. I like repair shops. Not the big gleaming appliance stores, but the small, cluttered, half-lit shops where someone has been fixing the same kinds of things for thirty years. The toaster hospital. The lamp clinic.
