This is England, I thought, and then immediately thought it was a stupid thought to have, and then thought that stupid thoughts are also part of the point. You have them, you discard them, you have better ones. The mind, when it is not being fed a constant stream of headlines and messages and instructions, begins to produce its own material, and some of it is nonsense, and some of it is surprisingly good.

I turned left at a footpath sign that pointed, optimistically, toward a village whose name I did not recognize. I had no reason to go that way except that the path was narrow and overgrown and looked like it wanted to be followed. This is the secret pleasure of walking nowhere: you can follow a path simply because it looks inviting, and nobody will ask you to justify it. The path took me along the edge of a wood, and the wood was mostly ash and sycamore, and the ash leaves were coming down in a slow, steady fall, each one turning as it fell, catching the light. I know almost nothing about trees, in the formal sense. I can identify an oak at a distance and a pine at a distance and that is about the limit of my expertise. But I know which trees I like to walk under. I like ash, because it feels kind. I like oak, because it feels ancient and unhurried. I do not particularly like sycamore, which feels a bit common and a bit bullying, spreading its seeds everywhere. These are not botanical judgments. They are walking judgments, and walking judgments are perfectly valid in their own way.

A woodpecker started up somewhere above me, laughing at his own joke. I stopped and listened. I could not see him, but I could hear exactly where he was, in that way that sound in a wood is both everywhere and pinpointed. A blackbird answered him from the other side of the path. For a minute I stood there in the wet and listened to two birds argue, and I felt, with a suddenness that surprised me, obscurely happy. Not thrilled, not ecstatic, just quietly, durably happy, in the way that you are happy when your hands are warm and you have nowhere to be for the next hour. I thought about how rarely I allow myself that state. I am generally either busy or tired, and busy and tired are not the same as happy, though they pretend to be its cousins.

The path came out by a river. It was not a big river. It was the kind of river that in summer would be shallow enough for children to paddle in and in winter would be brown and fast and a little frightening. Today it was somewhere in between, running clear and cold over stones that were green with algae. A kingfisher shot under a branch, a streak of impossible blue, and was gone before I could be sure I had seen it. I have seen kingfishers maybe four times in my life, and each time I have felt disproportionately lucky, as if I had been given a small, private gift by the universe. This is probably a misreading of how the universe works, but it is a pleasant misreading, and I see no reason to correct it.

On the bank sat an old man in a canvas jacket, with a fishing rod propped against a stick and a thermos on a small stool. He was not, as far as I could tell, catching anything. He was watching the water, which is, I suspect, the main point of fishing at his age, if fishing is still the word for it. "Any luck?" I asked, because it seemed rude not to.

"Not today," he said, without turning around. "They're being shy. Or I'm being boring. One of the two." He then told me, in a way that suggested he had been waiting all morning for someone to ask, that the river used to have trout in it, real trout, not the stocked ones, and that his father had fished it with a line made from a horsehair, and that the bridge ahead was built from stones taken from a quarry that closed in nineteen sixty-three. He knew the name of the quarry. He knew the name of the man who owned it. He knew which pub the quarrymen drank in. I knew none of this, and I probably will not remember most of it, but I listened, because listening to a man talk about a river he loves is a good use of a rainy afternoon.

We talked for perhaps ten minutes. He asked where I was going. I said I wasn't sure. He nodded, as if this were a perfectly respectable answer, and perhaps, in the economy of riverbanks, it is. He said, "Well, you'll get there anyway," which is both true and untrue, and which I have been turning over in my mind ever since. The river went on, indifferent to both of us, under the bridge and around the bend, toward a town I have also never lived in.

I walked on. The path went up a slight rise and then down again, and I came to a small village that consisted of about twenty houses, a church, a phone box that someone had turned into a little lending library, and a pub that was closed, or possibly just dark. It was three in the afternoon, which is an awkward time for a pub, neither lunch nor evening. I sat on a bench outside the church and ate an apple I had in my bag. The apple was bruised on one side and very sweet on the other. The churchyard had a yew tree in it that was older than the church, which in turn was older than the village, which was older than anyone could quite remember. I thought about time, as you do in churchyards, but not in a morbid way. More in the way of, "My, there is a lot of it, and most of us spend so much of it checking our watches."

Time is the great problem of modern walking. We have become so accustomed to filling time that empty time feels like a malfunction. If I stand still for more than a few seconds, I feel an urge to check my phone, not because I expect a message, but because stillness feels like an error message. I have to remind myself that stillness is not an error. It is, in fact, the state in which most of the interesting things happen. A heron stands perfectly still for a very long time, and then, in a movement so fast you almost miss it, it strikes. A tree stands still for a hundred years and drops its fruit. A man sits by a river and catches nothing and has a perfectly good afternoon. Stillness is not the opposite of action. It is action, cooled down.

At some point, walking nowhere, you begin to think about all the places you have walked somewhere, and how different they feel. Your childhood neighborhood, for example, which you walked every day to school and to the shops and to the park, and which you know in your feet better than in your mind. I grew up in a street with a steep hill and a corner shop that sold sherbet lemons and a lamppost that buzzed. I have not lived there for more than twenty years. When I go back, which is rarely, I am struck by how small everything is. The hill is not steep. The shop is a flat. The lamppost has been replaced. And yet my feet remember the hill as steep, and my mouth remembers the sherbet lemons as sharper than any sherbet lemon I have tasted since. Memory is a kind of walking, too, except you cannot choose the route and you keep taking wrong turns into rooms you had forgotten existed.

Walking helps memory, I think, because it gives memory a place to happen. Your mind is not good at remembering things in the abstract. It remembers them in context, in weather, in the company of other senses. That is why you can walk down a street you haven't been down in ten years and suddenly recall, with perfect clarity, a conversation you had while walking down it, and the exact quality of the light, and the fact that your shoes were leaking. The walk unlocks the filing cabinet. If you are always in a hurry, you never turn the key.

There is also the question of boredom, which is unfashionable to praise and which I think is underrated. We treat boredom as a problem to be solved, a gap to be filled with content. Content is the word we use now, which tells you something about our relationship to experience. We do not want to be bored, so we fill the bus ride, the queue, the walk, the waiting room, with small, bright, disposable diversions. And then we wonder why everything feels so thin. Boredom, properly tolerated, is not empty. It is the mind's way of clearing its throat. After a few minutes of being bored, your mind will start to do something interesting, because it cannot stand the vacuum. It will make a connection. It will remember a dream. It will think of a better way to phrase that email. It will notice the yew tree.

I am not arguing against phones, or buses, or appointments, or emails. I have appointments. I answer emails, sometimes even on time. I am arguing, if arguing is the word, for a certain proportion. For every hour of scheduled, optimized, content-filled time, perhaps we need ten minutes of scheduled, unoptimized, unfilled time. Ten minutes of walking nowhere. Ten minutes of sitting on a bench eating a bruised apple. Ten minutes in which nothing is accomplished and nothing is optimized and nothing is reported back to anyone. This is not productivity. This is maintenance. A garden that is never left alone grows weeds. A mind that is never left alone grows stale.

The rain came back, lightly, as I walked back toward the town by a different route, because a walk that goes out and comes back the same way feels like a smaller walk, even if it is the same distance. The fields were now a deep green, and sheep were huddled in the corners of them, looking, as sheep do, perpetually slightly damp and slightly judgmental. A little girl in a yellow raincoat was jumping in puddles with an enthusiasm that I envied. Her mother was standing under a tree, holding a plastic bag, watching, not rushing her. I thought, that mother has understood something. The puddles will dry. The girl will grow up and have appointments and emails. But today, the puddles are here, and she is here, and there is no reason to hurry her out of them.

I got back to town at about five, soaked to the knees, with mud on my shoes and a head full of useless, pleasant information about quarrymen and kingfishers and the habits of yew trees. I missed my appointment, or rather I was late for it, and the person I was meeting said, "Oh, we thought you'd had a car breakdown," and I said, "Something like that," which was not exactly a lie, because my car, in the sense of my own two legs, had indeed broken down, or rather had decided to go its own way for a while. She understood. People understand more than we think, if you give them a chance.

That evening I made tea and stood in my kitchen and looked out the window at the darkening street. My shoes were by the door, drying. My coat was over a chair. I felt tired in the good way, the way you feel after a long walk, which is different from the tired way you feel after a long day of sitting. The first kind of tiredness is in your legs. The second kind is in your eyes. I have spent a lot of my adult life being tired in my eyes. It was nice, for once, to be tired in my legs.

I did not have a revelation. I did not decide to sell my possessions and walk to the sea. I did not discover a new purpose. What I discovered, if the word is not too grand, was a reminder. A reminder that a town you have never lived in can still be interesting, that a river you will never fish in can still be worth watching, that an afternoon with no destination can still be an afternoon well spent. I had walked nowhere in particular, and I had arrived, precisely, nowhere in particular, which is to say I had arrived exactly where I needed to be, which is a sentence that sounds like nonsense until you have done it.

Tomorrow it will probably rain again. There will be buses, and appointments, and emails that need answering. But I think I will put my phone in my pocket, face down, and I will walk up the hill toward the fields, and I will see where the path goes, and I will let the apple be bruised on one side and sweet on the other.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
The Night Train

There is a particular kind of darkness that only exists on a train at night, and it is different from the darkness of a bedroom or a field or a city street after the shops have closed. It is a moving darkness, a darkness that travels with you and slides past the window in long, unbroken ribbons. I first understood this when I was fourteen and took the overnight train from Vienna to Venice with a school friend, both of us pretending not to be nervous, both of us clutching paper tickets that had already softened in our hands. The station had been bright and even frantic, full of announcements in three languages and the clatter of luggage trolleys, but once the wheels began to turn the whole world seemed to lower its voice. The lamps of the platform fell away one by one, and what replaced them was not blackness exactly but a deep, companionable quiet in which the click of the rails became a kind of heartbeat.

I have thought about that heartbeat many times since, in airports and on motorways and in apartments where the heating ticks through the night. A night train does not hurry in the way an aeroplane hurries, and it does not surrender to traffic in the way a car does. It keeps to its own schedule, older than any of its passengers, and it asks you to surrender to its schedule in return. You cannot get off in the middle of nowhere simply because you have changed your mind. You cannot check your position on a map every thirty seconds and feel reassured. You commit yourself, for eight or ten or fourteen hours, to a line drawn across a continent by people who lived before you were born, and you allow that line to carry you while you do almost nothing at all. That almost nothing is the point. In a life measured by notifications and deadlines, the enforced idleness of a night train feels like a small, radical gift.

I took my first one with almost no luggage, just a rucksack and a book I never opened. I take them now with more luggage than I need and the same book, still unopened, tucked into the side pocket as a kind of talisman. The habits change, but the feeling of departure does not. There is always a moment, just after the doors close, when you realize that the decision has been made. The train eases out of the station, it gathers speed, it passes the last signals and the last suburbs, and the world you knew a minute ago is already behind you. Strangers who were jostling beside you on the platform settle into seats opposite or above you, and for a while you are all bound together by a shared temporary address. You are no longer in any particular city. You are in transit, and transit has its own rules and its own small rituals.

One of those rituals is the dining car, which on many night trains still follows the old pattern of white tablecloths, weighted cutlery, and a menu printed as if the year were still 1974. I have eaten in dining cars in France, in Romania, in Vietnam, and in Scotland, and the food has varied wildly, but the atmosphere has remained recognizably the same. There is a sense of occasion that cannot be faked. You dress, almost unconsciously, a little better for dinner. You sit up straighter. You lower your voice. You accept that the meal will take longer than it would in a restaurant on the ground, because the train will sway and the stewards will have to move carefully and nobody wants to be in a hurry when the landscape is already doing all the moving. I once had dinner on a train crossing the Hungarian plain in late October, and the chef, who spoke no English and very little German, brought me a bowl of goulash that was the color of brick and tasted of paprika and patience. Outside, the plain was invisible, but I could feel its flatness in the way the train ran, straight and unhurried, as if it too knew there was nothing to climb and nothing to avoid.

The dining car is also where the train reveals itself as a small society. In a plane everyone faces forward and minds their own business. In a train, especially at night, people face each other. They offer each other salt. They comment on the weather in a country they are passing through without stopping. They ask where you are going, and you ask them, and for a few minutes you share a version of your life that is slightly more honest than the one you would offer in an office. I met a retired schoolteacher from Krakow on a train to Prague who told me, between courses, that she had been traveling to see her granddaughter every month for twelve years, and that she always took the night train because she liked to fall asleep to the sound of the wheels and wake up already in the city, as if she had been given those hours for free. I met two students from Lyon who were going to a music festival and who shared their bread and cheese and a bottle of wine that they opened with a key, because they had forgotten a corkscrew. I met a man who worked as a signalman and who could tell, by the rhythm of the train, exactly where we were, even when the windows were black and there was nothing to see but our own reflections.

That reflection is another thing that belongs to night trains. The carriage windows become mirrors when it is dark outside. You see yourself, suddenly, in the glass, lit from within by the soft yellow light of the lamps. You are not the crisp image you present in a photograph. You are slightly blurred, slightly tired, a little older than you thought. Beside your reflection, if you look carefully, you can sometimes see the reflection of the person sitting across from you, and then your two reflections overlap in a way that feels strangely intimate. I have spent whole journeys watching those ghostly double images pass over the landscape, lands that I could not see and therefore had to imagine. Hills, rivers, small towns, fields full of sleeping animals — all of them were out there in the dark, but the train kept them at arm’s length, offering only the occasional glimmer of a farmhouse light or the red eye of a signal far in the distance. The night train therefore creates a peculiar kind of geography, one made not of what you see but of what you infer from speed, from sound, from the pauses at stations where doors hiss and a stationmaster’s whistle is swallowed by the cold.

Sleep, of course, is the central promise of the night train, and it is also its biggest disappointment. Not everyone sleeps well on a train. The bunks are narrow, the pillows are thin, the corridor lights leak under the doors, and the person in the next compartment may snore in a key that does not match your own. And yet there is a quality to train sleep that is unlike sleep anywhere else. You are rocked, almost imperceptibly, from side to side, and the rocking is accompanied by a low, continuous hum that fills the silence between the clicks of the wheels. It is not silence at all, but a kind of white noise made by steel on steel, and over time it becomes so familiar that its absence would be more disturbing than its presence. I have slept in trains in India with the windows open to the warm night air, and in trains in Sweden with the windows sealed against the snow, and in both cases I woke with the strange conviction that I had been carried rather than that I had traveled. My body had moved hundreds of miles, but my mind had stayed in one place, turning over the same few thoughts, dreaming in short loops that ended whenever the train slowed for a junction.

There is a special pleasure, too, in waking up at an unexpected hour and finding the train stopped at a station you have never heard of. The doors may be open, the platform may be empty, the station clock may show a time that belongs to no one in particular. A cat may be sitting on a bench. A vending machine may be humming to itself. For a few minutes the train belongs to that place, and that place belongs, briefly, to you. Then the guard blows his whistle, the doors close, and you are moving again, carrying the brief stillness with you like a souvenir. I remember waking somewhere outside Ljubljana and seeing, through the fogged window, a woman selling flowers from a bucket, even though it was three in the morning and the flowers were pale blue and looked, in the station light, almost luminous. I did not buy any, of course. I could not. But the image stayed with me all night, and when I finally arrived in the morning, I found myself describing that woman to anyone who would listen, as if she were the real destination and the city at the end of the line were merely an excuse to meet her.

Borders are another feature of night trains that aeroplanes have made almost obsolete, and they give the night train a dignity that it would otherwise lack. On a plane you cross a border in your sleep without knowing it, and you wake up to find that the cabin crew have changed their language and the safety instructions are printed in a different alphabet. On a train, a border is an event. The train slows, sometimes it stops for a long time, the lights in the corridor come on, and a uniformed officer walks through the carriage, looking at passports with a tired, methodical patience. People wake up, they fumble for documents, they apologize for the state of their hair, they make jokes about the weather. If the border is between countries that use different gauges or different electrical systems, the whole train may have to be lifted or shunted or reattached to a different locomotive, and the night is broken into stages. The slowness is absurd, if you measure it by efficiency, but it is honest. It admits that countries are real things, that they have edges, and that crossing from one to another is not a matter of pressing a button but of waiting, and being checked, and being allowed through.

I crossed from Germany into Poland once at a time when the train stopped for nearly an hour, and during that hour a whole subculture formed in the corridor. Someone produced a deck of cards. Someone else produced a thermos of tea. A man who had been asleep in the bunk opposite mine emerged in his socks and stood in the doorway of his compartment, talking to anyone who passed. We talked about football and about the price of bread and about the strange persistence of certain kinds of bureaucracy. Nobody was in a hurry, because there was nowhere to hurry to. The train could not leave until the paperwork was done, and the paperwork would be done when it was done. When we finally set off again, the mood in the carriage was lighter, as if we had all survived something together. The border had divided us from the next country, but in the small space of the train it had united us with each other.

That sense of accidental community is, I think, what I miss most when I travel by other means. Cars seal you in. Planes lift you out. Night trains keep you in close, slightly uncomfortable contact with strangers who may become, for a night, your companions. You share a toilet that is never quite clean. You share the frustration when the heating is too hot or too cold. You share the good news when someone’s phone finally finds a signal and they get a message they have been waiting for. You learn the small geography of the carriage: which windows rattle, which doors stick, which seats are best for watching the sunrise. The conductor becomes a familiar figure, moving through the train with a lantern or a ticket punch, checking on people, reassuring the anxious, waking those who have asked to be woken. In old films the conductor is a romantic figure, a man who knows every station and every passenger by name. In real life he is usually tired and overworked, but he still carries a certain authority that comes from being in charge of a small, moving world.

There is also the matter of arrival, which on a night train is never quite as simple as stepping off a plane and into a terminal. You arrive in the middle of a city, often at a grand station built when trains were the glory of an age, and you arrive at a speed that allows you to see the city before you are fully in it. The train slows through the suburbs, it passes allotments and workshops and apartment blocks with their laundry hanging out, and by the time it pulls into the station you have already begun to adjust to the new place. The light is different. The air smells different. The language of the announcements is different. But you have not been jolted there. You have been eased there, like a boat coming into a harbor. I have arrived in Vienna at dawn, in Budapest in the rain, in Hanoi in a heat that felt like opening an oven door, and in each case the city seemed to accept me rather than inspect me. I stepped down onto the platform with my bag, feeling travel-worn but not travel-battered, and the city carried on around me as if I had always lived there.

Afterwards, there is always a curious afterimage. For the rest of the day, your body remembers the rocking. When you stand still in a queue or sit at a desk, you feel a faint sway, as if the train were still moving beneath you. Sounds that resemble the click of wheels — a dripping tap, a clock ticking, the hum of a refrigerator — bring back the night. You find yourself missing the low background noise of the carriage, and you might even catch yourself looking for the conductor in a crowd, expecting someone to punch your ticket and tell you that everything is under control. This afterimage is not unpleasant. It is a reminder that you have been somewhere other than where you started, and that you have allowed yourself to be carried there without managing every detail. In a world that encourages us to curate our experiences, to photograph them, to rate them, to share them in real time, the night train offers an older kind of travel, one in which you surrender a little of your control and receive, in return, a story that you cannot entirely tell because much of it happened while you were asleep.

I am aware that night trains are disappearing in some places, replaced by faster, more efficient daytime services, or abandoned altogether in favor of low-cost flights. I understand the economics. It is hard to justify a service that runs once a night with a dining car and sleeping compartments when a plane can carry more people faster and for less money. But I also think something is lost when we remove the night from travel. The night is not an obstacle to be overcome. It is a part of experience that deserves its own kind of journey. To travel at night is to accept that you will not see everything, that you will miss the landscape, that you will have to trust the engineers and the drivers and the timetable. It is to accept that arrival is not the only valuable moment. The journey itself, with its lights and its shadows, its strangers and its small kindnesses, is worth preserving for its own sake.

I still take the night train whenever I can. I book a seat in a couchette, I pack a book I probably will not read, I bring a bottle of water and a sweater because the heating is unpredictable. I arrive at the station a little early, because I like the feeling of anticipation, and I watch the train come in, nose first, like an animal returning to a den. I find my compartment, I make my bed, I settle in. When the train moves, I do not work on my laptop or scroll through my phone. I watch the window. I listen to the wheels. I let the darkness do its work. And when I wake, somewhere between the place I left and the place I am going, I feel, for a brief and unreasonable moment, that I have been given a night for free, a night that belongs to nobody else, a night that can be spent simply being carried from here to there, in the company of strangers, under a sky full of stars that are mostly hidden by the roof of the train, but that are there all the same, waiting for the morning.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Department of Unfinished Things**

There is a room on the seventh floor of the Municipal Records Building that does not officially exist. If you take the elevator from the lobby, the buttons go 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8. There is no 7. Press 8 and get out halfway, if you know how to listen for the pause between floors, and you will find a corridor that smells faintly of old paper and rain, even when it has not rained, because the windows at the end of the hall look out onto a courtyard that never gets sun. At the end of that corridor is a door with frosted glass, and in small brass letters it says, OFFICE OF DEFERRED COMPLETION. Underneath, in someone's ballpoint, added years ago and never removed, someone has written: *We do not finish. We witness.*

I have worked there for eleven years. My title, according to the city, is Senior Keeper, Grade III. My name is June. I have a desk, a stamp, a kettle that whistles too loudly, and a set of keys that open more doors than the building seems to have. My job is not complicated, and it is also impossible to explain at dinner parties, which is why I have learned to tell people I work in archives. That is not a lie. It is a simplification, the way a map is a simplification. A map leaves out most of the world so that you can find your way around the part that remains.

The building itself is unfinished, which feels appropriate. The east wing was planned in 1962, budgeted in 1974, begun in 1981, and abandoned in 1987 when the money ran out and the mayor who had promised it fell out of favor. The concrete stops mid-wall. Pigeons nest in the rebar. From the courtyard you can see the stairs going up to a floor that was never built, and sometimes in the winter the wind makes a low note through the hollow pipes, like a cello being tuned in another room. The Department of Unfinished Things was housed there because, as Mr. Patel in Personnel told me on my first day, "Who else would want it?" It was a joke, but it was also a kind of wisdom the city stumbles into now and then.

People find us. They almost never look surprised to be there. I used to think that was strange — a woman carrying a half-knitted sweater in a grocery bag, a man in a suit carrying a wooden boat hull under one arm as if it were a briefcase, a teenager with a friendship bracelet with one end longer than the other — but I have come to understand that most people know, long before they arrive, that they have been carrying something they started and did not stop, and did not finish, and cannot quite throw away. They bring it to us the way you bring a coat to a tailor, not expecting miracles, only care.

Our intake form is simple. One page. Object: ____. Started: ____. Stopped: ____. Reason for stopping, if you know it: ____. Reason for bringing it here: ____. Name and telephone number: ____. There is a line at the bottom that says, *Completion is not required. Continuation is not promised.* I make people read that line out loud, not because I am cruel, but because it changes the air in the room. Shoulders drop. Colleagues in other departments rush. We slow down.

Mrs. Alvarez came in on a Tuesday, which is our busiest day, because people seem to do their reckonings on Mondays and bring the evidence on Tuesdays. She was eighty-two, with hair in a tight silver bun and a purse that snapped shut with authority. She set a crossword puzzle on my desk, folded soft as cloth from being handled. It was dated, in pencil in the corner, 1979. "43 across," she said. "I have been thinking about 43 across for forty-six years. It is a seven-letter word. It means the thing you feel when you almost remember something." She smiled. "I still do not know it." I stamped it and put it on Shelf 12, which is for Mental Puzzles Abandoned Mid-Question, between a half-solved Rubik's Cube and a chess game where White has walked into a trap and Black has not noticed. Mrs. Alvarez wept a little when I gave her a receipt. "You are the first person," she said, "who has ever thought this was important enough to file."

The man with the boat hull was named Elias. He was fifty, and his hands were rough from rope and varnish. He had been building a sailboat in his garage for twenty years. Every spring he would sand it. Every autumn he would stop. "My son was supposed to help me launch it," he said. "He moved to Oregon. He has a baby now. He says we can launch it when the baby is old enough to help." He laughed, and it was not a bitter laugh. "That is a long time to wait for a boat." We put the hull in Bay 3, where the large things live: a piano with thirteen keys, a dressmaker's dummy with one arm missing, a bicycle with no chain. Elias visits it on the first Sunday of every month. He sits on a stool we keep for that purpose and talks to it, and sometimes he brings a sandwich and eats it in its company. He told me once that the boat does not feel abandoned. "It feels like it is resting," he said. "There is a difference."

Our shelves are organized not by type but by decade of abandonment. The 1950s are quiet and dusty and smell of tobacco. People from that era, when they left things, tended to leave them neatly, with instructions. The 1960s are louder; almost everything there hums. The 1970s are optimistic, full of things that were meant to change the world in small, practical ways — a solar-powered toaster, a novel about a lighthouse keeper who collects feelings, a community garden that was planted but never weeded. The 1980s are reflective and a little melancholy. The 1990s are earnest, full of half-written screenplays and businesses that were going to be different. The 2000s sprawl. Everything from the last twenty years asks to be digitally backed up, as if that would make it more finished, which it does not. The present decade is the smallest, because we are still pretending we will finish things this year.

We have rules, few and strict. We do not finish things. We do not start things. We do not judge things. We tag them, we store them, we check on them. Some require water. A small fern started as a houseplant and abandoned on a windowsill lives on my desk and is doing better than most houseplants. Some require music. A violin that was left mid-piece prefers the radio on low in the afternoon. Some seeds leak out of envelopes if you are not careful. Some things, if you put them next to other unfinished things, begin to talk to each other in ways I cannot describe without sounding fanciful, though I have worked here long enough to know that fanciful is not the same as false. A letter that needs an answer will, if placed near a question, sometimes grow a postscript all on its own. We do not encourage this. We simply note it in the log.

Every now and then, something finishes itself. This is the strangest part of the job, and the part I have never been able to write up in a report without Personnel sending it back with a note that says, "Please restate in administrative language." A quilt that was last touched in 1998 was found one morning complete, every square sewn, the backing turned and stitched. No one had signed it out. A couple who had left an unfinished argument in a sealed envelope in 2011 returned, asked for it back, read it together in the waiting area, and left holding hands, the envelope empty. A song that had been stuck on its second verse for a decade arrived back in the mail with the final verse added in a different handwriting. We do not claim credit. We simply file the finished things in a separate room, which we call, with great originality, the Finished Room. It is brighter in there. The air feels lighter. People who work near it tend to hum without knowing why.

In my bottom desk drawer, I keep my own unfinished thing. I have kept it there since before I worked here, since before I was qualified to keep anything. It is a letter. It begins, "Dear Dad," and then, on the next line, "I think I am writing this because..." and then it stops. I was eighteen when I started it. I was angry, and then I was hurt, and then I was embarrassed, and then I was grown, and every few years I would take it out and read it and add nothing. It lives in an envelope with a stamp from a post office that closed a long time ago. Some days I think I am keeping it unfinished out of respect for him. Some days I think I am keeping it unfinished out of cowardice. Most days I think the truth is in between, which is where most truths live, quietly, in the unfinished room of a person.

The rule, as you will have guessed, is that I cannot finish it here. I cannot bring my own things to my own desk and stamp them and put them on a shelf and call that honesty. So it stays in the drawer, and I check on it the way I check on everything else. Sometimes I hear it rustle. Once, I opened the drawer and found that a single word had been added underneath, in my own handwriting, but I have no memory of writing it. The word was "sorry." I do not know if it was there before. I do not know if I wrote it in my sleep. I left it. It felt important not to erase a word whose author I could not identify.

Last spring, on a Thursday when the rain had been falling sideways since dawn, a boy arrived with his mother. He was about nine, with a backpack too big for him and a notebook clutched to his chest like a shield. His mother did the talking at first. "His teacher," she said, "assigned free writing. She said, 'Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.' He has been staring at the page for three days. He cried last night. He said he doesn't know what he wants." The boy did not cry now. He looked at my desk, at the stamp, at the plant, at the shelves that went back beyond sight. "Are you a library?" he asked.

"Not exactly," I said.

"Do you have books that are finished?" he asked.

"We have many kinds of things," I said, "and we try to be kind to all of them."

He opened the notebook. The first page was blank except for his name in careful block letters at the top, NOAH, and underneath, in smaller letters, as if he were apologizing for the size of the assignment, 2500 WORDS. He had drawn a small line under it, as if to contain it. "What if I don't want to write about anything?" he said. "Is that allowed?"

His mother put a hand on his shoulder. "We told him people bring unfinished things here," she said. "He wanted to bring his."

I took the notebook, because that is what we do. We take things gently and we say, we will keep this safe. We stamped the intake form. Object: Notebook. Started: Three days ago. Stopped: Immediately. Reason for stopping: Did not know what he wanted. Reason for bringing it here: Teacher said write freely. I wrote nothing else. I put it on Shelf 1, which is for things that have not yet become what they are, and I gave Noah a receipt, which he folded very carefully and put in his pocket.

He lingered, though. Most people linger a little, even when they think they are ready to go. He looked at the boat hull in Bay 3. He looked at the fern. "Does it grow?" he asked.

"Slowly," I said.

"Does it mind?"

"I don't think minding is the right word," I said, "but I think it is glad to be here."

Noah nodded as if I had answered a question he had been saving up. "Can I come see it again?" he asked. "The notebook, I mean. Not the fern. Well, the fern too, if that's okay."

"Of course," I said. "It will be here."

That night, after the building emptied and the security guard made his rounds with his flashlight, I stayed late. The rain had stopped. The courtyard was glistening. I told myself I was doing inventory, which is true, and also not the whole truth, which is also true. I walked the shelves with my clipboard, as I always do, and when I came to Shelf 1, I stopped in front of Noah's notebook. It was a plain blue notebook, the kind that costs very little and lasts forever. I should not have opened it. Opening is not in the rules. But some rules are about not finishing, and some are about not interfering, and I have learned over eleven years that there is a third category, which is about care, and care sometimes looks very much like a small, rule-breaking act done quietly and without witness.

I opened it to the first page. Under NOAH and 2500 WORDS, someone — it could only have been me, though I do not remember deciding to do it — had written one sentence, in blue ink, in handwriting that was mine and also not quite mine: *This is about a boy who was asked to write freely, and he didn't know what he wanted, so he went to a room that keeps unfinished things, and he left his notebook there, and hoped it would learn how to want something on its own.*

I stared at it for a long time. I do not know if I wrote it that afternoon, or if I have been writing it, in pieces, for years without realizing. I closed the notebook. I put it back exactly where I had found it, at a slight angle, the way Noah had left it on my desk. I turned off the lights in the office. I locked the door. I walked down the corridor that should not be there, and pressed the elevator button for 8, and went down to the lobby, where the ordinary world resumed its ordinary business of people coming and going through revolving doors.

I have thought about that sentence often since. About how easily a single sentence can turn an ending into a beginning, or rather, turn a stopping into a resting. 2500 words is a strange number. It is too many to be a sentence and too few to be a life. It is a size that says, you have room, but not forever. Free writing, I have come to believe, is not about saying everything. It is about giving a thought enough room to find its own shape, without you standing over it with a ruler. Children know this instinctively. They draw a house with the sun in the corner, because the sun belongs in the corner when you are starting. Adults forget. We start in the middle and try to be impressive. We try to finish before we have begun.

Later that week, a man came in with an apology he had been carrying for thirty years. It was not on paper. It was in his posture, in the way he held his hands. "I said something to my brother," he said. "It was untrue, and I knew it was untrue, and I said it anyway because I was young and wanted to win." He did not want us to store it. He wanted to know if there was a way to un-say it. I told him, as gently as I could, that we do not have a department for that. We have a department for things that are paused. Un-saying is not pausing. It is something else. It is, perhaps, a different kind of work, done in a different room, with different tools. He nodded. "I will go and see him," he said. "He is in a home now. He may not know me. I will bring the apology with me anyway. I will say it into the air if I have to." I watched him go, and I thought about how many finished things are really just unfinished things that have learned to be carried differently.

People sometimes ask me, usually at the end of a visit, when they are putting on their coats, whether I think their thing will ever be finished. It is the question everyone wants to ask and no one wants to hear the answer to, because the answer is not yes or no. The answer is: it will become what it becomes, and that may look like finishing from some angles and like resting from others, and both may be true at the same time. A conversation that lasts a lifetime is not unfinished because it never concluded. A garden is not unfinished because you pull weeds forever. A walk along a coastline is not unfinished because you turn back before the map runs out. Some things are meant to end, and some are meant to be left open, like a door in summer, so that air can move through.

At five o'clock, I do my rounds. I check that the fern has been watered. I check that the violin is not too lonely. I check that the boat hull is level on its supports. I sign the log. I turn off the kettle. I lock the cabinet where the stamps live. The building makes its evening sounds — pipes, distant traffic, the pigeons settling on the unfinished wing. I think about the shelves, all those paused lives, all those almosts and not-yets and maybes, waiting not for someone to complete them, but for someone to witness them long enough that they feel less alone in their incompleteness.

Somewhere on Shelf 1, in a plain blue notebook, there is a boy's name and a number and one sentence that begins a story about a boy who did not know what he wanted. It is waiting for the second sentence. It does not know if Noah will come back to write it, or if someone else will, or if it will sit there for years, growing slowly like a fern, glad to be there. It does not need to know. That is the secret the Department of Unfinished Things keeps, stamped in blue ink on every receipt we issue: you do not have to finish to be kept. You do not have to know what you want to be allowed to want something. You can begin, and stop, and rest, and begin again, and all of those are honest ways to move through a life.

The elevator will take me down to 1, and I will walk home under whatever sky the city has provided that night, and in the morning I will come back, and the door will be there, and the shelves will be there, and the kettle will whistle too loudly, and someone new will arrive carrying something they started a long time ago, or three days ago, or just now, in the elevator, on the way up to a floor that does not officially exist. I will take it gently. I will stamp it. I will say, we will keep this safe. And somewhere, in the quiet, the unfinished thing will hear itself being named, and for the first time in a long time, it will feel like a beginning again.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
Notes on a Day Spent Wandering

I woke up this morning before the alarm, which is something that almost never happens, and lay there for a while listening to the house settle into itself. The radiator ticked once, as if clearing its throat, and somewhere downstairs the fridge hummed its low, indifferent note, and through the thin curtains I could see that the light had that pale, washed-out quality which promises either a very fine day or a day that will rain in the most sideways and uncommitted way possible. I did not reach for my phone. It was an effort, a small, deliberate act of disobedience, and I noticed how my hand twitched toward the bedside table even as my mind told it not to. Instead I made tea, stood by the kitchen window with the mug warming my palms, and watched a neighbor unlock his bicycle and wheel it, thoughtfully, to the end of his drive, where he seemed to reconsider the entire enterprise and wheel it back again. There was no urgency in anything, and for the first time in weeks that felt like a gift rather than a failure.

The strange guilt of unscheduled time is something I have only lately learned to name. As an adult, most of my hours arrive pre-claimed, assigned a purpose and a metric, and even my leisure is usually optimized, measured in steps or finished pages or episodes watched, as if rest itself had to justify its existence by producing some evidence of improvement. To have a day with no appointment in it feels faintly scandalous, like skipping a meeting with myself. I kept catching an impulse to invent a task, to clean the skirting boards or reorganize the pantry or finally answer those emails that have been sitting in my inbox like unopened letters from a more responsible version of me. But I decided, perhaps out of laziness and perhaps out of a dawning curiosity, to let the day remain unclaimed, to see what would happen if I simply walked out of the front door and followed whatever caught my eye. It was not a grand experiment. It was merely a willingness to be led by small things.

Maps are a wonderful and terrible invention. They give you the illusion that a place is known once its outline is familiar, that to have traced a route a dozen times is to have understood it. I have walked these streets for years, more or less, and I can get from the bakery to the bus stop to the library without looking up, following the grooves worn into my habits. But this morning I left the map in my head at home. I turned down a lane I have always meant to explore but never have, a narrow passage between two houses where the pavement dips and the bins are always out and a cat, a fat marmalade cat, sits with great seriousness on a wall. I had always assumed it was a dead end, a service alley with nothing at the end of it but more bins. Today I discovered it opens, after a squeeze past a leaning fence, onto a small courtyard where someone grows tomatoes in a row of identical tin cans, and where the washing lines of three houses cross in a bright, tangled geometry overhead. It was not beautiful, exactly, but it was alive in a way my familiar route was not.

Childhood wandering was different because the world was sized for it. Then, a street could go on forever, and an afternoon could be an entire civilization of forts and expeditions and grievous injuries sustained in the line of duty. I remember the deep seriousness with which we planned those expeditions, the hand-drawn maps with X marking places that were, in reality, a shrub and a discarded sofa, the solemn oaths not to return home until signals were sent or supplies ran out. We were not killing time; we were inhabiting it completely, the way you inhabit a house you have just moved into and are still learning the creaks of. Somewhere along the way, walking became transportation rather than exploration, a means of getting from one point to another with maximum efficiency and minimum deviation, and the world narrowed to corridors. I think I missed the feeling of a place being larger than my errands, and perhaps that is why I was excited, in a quiet and slightly embarrassed way, by the prospect of being a flâneur in my own neighborhood.

The town I live in is a coastal town, which is a particular kind of place with its own weather and its own temperament. The sea is always present even when you cannot see it, in the salt that stiffens a coat, in the cries of gulls that sound perpetually outraged about something, in the way the light changes at four in the afternoon as if someone had turned a dial. The town has the usual mixture of pride and neglect that comes from being somewhere people pass through on their way to somewhere more famous. There are grand Victorian houses with peeling paint and elegant proportions, and there are buildings from the sixties that look like they were designed by someone who had only heard of architecture described to them secondhand. The harbor is mostly pleasure boats now, bobbing and nudging each other in the swell, and the old fish market is a café with a chalkboard that misspells scones. None of it is pristine, and that is precisely its charm; it has the look of a place that has been loved intermittently, by different generations, in different ways.

I walked down to the harbor first, because the sea has a way of rearranging your thoughts. The tide was out, leaving a wide expanse of wet sand and stranded rock pools that glittered like something dropped and forgotten. An old man in waders was hunting for something with a bucket and a fork, moving slowly and with great concentration, as if the shore were a library and he were looking for a particular book. A woman was walking two dogs of wildly different sizes, one of them trotting with enormous dignity and the other apparently convinced that every lamp post contained a secret worth investigating. The wind came off the water in sudden, companionable gusts, lifting the corners of my coat and carrying with it the smell of salt and diesel and, faintly, chips. I stood for a while and did nothing in particular, which is to say I watched the boats strain at their moorings and the gulls perform their aerial disputes, and I tried to remember the last time I had stood somewhere simply to be in it, rather than to pass through it on the way to a better view.

The baker was halfway through his first batch when I arrived, and the warm, yeasty air spilled out onto the pavement each time the door opened. Inside, the counter was a small museum of brownness, rolls and loaves and buns in every shade from pale gold to near-black, arranged with a care that suggested both pride and an understanding that people do choose with their eyes first. I bought a roll and a coffee, though I did not need either, and took them to sit on the low wall outside, where a sparrow hopped around my feet with an optimism that bordered on delusion. The baker came out with a tray of something hot and dusted it with flour, and we exchanged the kind of brief, weather-based conversation that is the small change of community. He told me the ovens had been temperamental all week, that the sea air got into everything, that his father had baked in this same shop and had claimed the rolls rose better when it rained. I told him I hoped that was true, because the forecast looked promising, and he laughed and said the weather was the only thing in town that kept its promises, and even then only by accident.

Small conversations are a kind of currency that has been devalued by our reluctance to spend it. We have become so practiced at moving through public space with our attention elsewhere, earbuds in, eyes forward, that a stranger speaking to us feels like an interruption rather than an invitation. But today I found myself in several of them, and each one altered the texture of the day in a way I had not anticipated. A woman in the bookshop asked what I was reading, and when I said I was not, strictly speaking, reading anything at the moment, she took this as a challenge and recommended three books with the enthusiasm of a missionary. In the post office, a man behind me in the queue asked if I knew whether the parcel service had improved, and we spent five minutes elaborating a shared theory that nothing had improved since approximately 1987. None of these exchanges were significant. All of them were human in a way that left me feeling less like a solitary figure moving through a painted backdrop and more like a resident of an actual place, temporarily borrowed by an actual community.

The bookshop is not, technically, a bookshop anymore. It is a secondhand bookshop and a record shop and a place where someone sells handmade soap and a place where, on Saturdays, a man tunes pianos in the back room. It has the wonderful, musty smell of paper and dust and old wood, and the shelves lean at angles that suggest decades of gentle surrender. I went in with no intention of buying anything and emerged, as always, with a biography of a lighthouse keeper, a poetry collection with a cracked spine, and a novel I had already read twice but which I somehow felt needed rescuing from the classics table. The joy of such a place is its total indifference to algorithm and relevance. No one has optimized the stock for my demographic. The books are there because someone, at some point, decided to keep them, and the order is mostly alphabetical except where it is mostly by size, and except where it is neither. I spent an hour pulling volumes out at random and reading the first paragraph, that small, arbitrary act of judgment which has led me astray more reliably than any other in my life. There was a book about weather, which seemed appropriate, and a book about the history of walking, which seemed like a taunt, and a children's book about a bear who wanted to be a lighthouse. I bought the one about weather.

Boredom, I am coming to believe, is a vastly underrated state of mind. We treat it as a problem to be solved instantly with a screen, a podcast, a quick scroll through the evidence that other people are having more interesting lives and different kinds of cake. But boredom has a useful function; it is the mind's way of clearing its throat and asking what, exactly, it is doing here. When I am bored, my thoughts slow down and begin to wander in ways they do not when I am occupied, and they make connections that feel less like productivity and more like discovery. Today, sitting on a bench because my feet had decided they had done enough for the moment, I found my mind drifting from the price of cheese to the design of benches to the fact that I had never once, in all my years here, actually sat on this particular bench, though I had passed it a thousand times. I watched the clouds arrange themselves into temporary continents and watched a cyclist struggle with a child seat and watched, with great interest, the progress of a small ladybird making its way across the armrest. It was not a wasted half hour. It was, I think, the most productive thing I did all day, though nothing I could list on a form would capture it.

By late morning the rain had arrived, as forecast and as promised. It did not come in a dramatic downpour but in a fine, persistent mist that softened all the edges and turned the streets into shining versions of themselves. I took shelter under the awning of a closed shop, where a poster advertising a lost cat had been curling in the damp for what looked like a year, and where a small group of us, strangers to one another, performed the elaborate choreography of people pretending not to be waiting for the same thing. A woman with a shopping trolley and a very determined umbrella, a schoolboy with a plastic bag held over his hair, an elderly man walking a dachshund in a knitted coat. The rain made us temporary conspirators. The schoolboy asked the elderly man if his dog was cold, and the elderly man said the dog was always cold, that it was a breed preference, and that in any case the coat was his wife's idea and the dog had strong feelings about it. We all laughed at this, and the rain seemed, briefly, like a shared joke rather than an inconvenience. When it eased, we went our separate ways with an odd sense of having been in something together.

I had lunch in a small café that seats six people and serves soup that changes depending on the mood of the person making it. Today it was lentil, thick enough to stand a spoon in, with bread that had been toasted and then, perhaps as an afterthought, buttered. I sat by the window and watched the wet street and read the first chapter of my rescued novel, and I was gratified by the way a good book can make a small room feel larger, as if the walls had been politely asked to move back a little. The owner, who knows my face but not, as far as I can tell, my name, brought over an extra roll without being asked and said it was going stale, which was clearly a lie of the most benevolent kind. I ate slowly. There is a particular pleasure in eating a meal without a screen, without a schedule, without the sense that the fork is competing with a clock. The soup was hot and the rain had stopped and for a moment the whole world narrowed to the steam rising from the bowl and the comfortable weight of a book in my pocket, and I felt, in a way I rarely do, entirely present in my own life.

In the afternoon I went to the post office to post a letter I had written two days ago and which had been sitting on the mantelpiece developing a sense of entitlement. It was a real letter, on paper, in an envelope, with a stamp that cost more than I remembered stamps costing, which led to a brief and silent reckoning with time. The letter was to a friend who lives in another country and who communicates, as I do, mostly in the brief, apologetic messages that accumulate in the spaces between our actual lives. Writing it had taken me an evening, and I had crossed out whole sentences and started again, trying to find a tone that was neither too formal nor too casual, which is, I suspect, the entire difficulty of saying anything true to anyone. Posting it felt like releasing something into a slower system, one that would take days to move across continents and that would arrive, eventually, in a physical form that could be held and put on a fridge and returned to. I was absurdly pleased with myself, in the way one is pleased with a child who has learned to tie a shoe: a small competence, long delayed, finally accomplished.

After that I climbed the hill, because a walk that does not include a hill feels incomplete, like a story without a middle. The path goes up between allotments where people grow things with more enthusiasm than skill, and past a graveyard where the oldest stones lean at dramas angles, and then it emerges onto the common, a wide, windy expanse of grass that belongs to everyone and to no one. From the top you can see the whole town arranged like a model of itself: the harbor, the Victorian houses, the sixties blocks, the church spire puncturing the sky like a punctuation mark. The view has the curious effect of making my concerns smaller without making them less real. The emails and the deadlines and the vague sense of falling behind were still there, somewhere below, but from this height they looked like what they were, which is to say temporary arrangements made by a person who had, for the moment, decided to arrange things differently. The wind was strong and the grass bent in waves, and I stood there with my hands in my pockets feeling, briefly and completely, like a figure in a landscape painting, which is not a bad way to feel on a Tuesday.

Children were playing on the common, in that loose, unorganized way that seems to have survived despite all our best efforts to schedule it out of existence. They had invented a game involving a stick, a ball, and a set of rules that changed every three minutes in response to injustice. There was a dispute about whether the stick was magic or merely a stick, and a solemn negotiation about boundaries, and a moment of high drama when the ball rolled into a bush and was declared, by unanimous vote, to have been stolen by a dragon. I watched them for a while from a distance, not because I am particularly nostalgic for childhood, which I remember as being mostly a series of minor humiliations and excellent snacks, but because there is something clarifying about watching people who have not yet learned to apologize for taking up space. They were loud and inefficient and utterly absorbed, and the game was entirely pointless, and that was precisely why it mattered. I thought about how many of my own activities are designed to be useful, and how few of them produce the kind of joy that comes from making something up and then believing in it completely for an afternoon.

I stopped at the lighthouse on my way back down, though it is not a working lighthouse anymore and has been a museum and a café and, for a brief period in the eighties, a disco, according to a plaque that seemed to be trying not to dwell on the matter. The museum itself was closed, but the tower was open, and I climbed the winding stairs in the company of a school group who were asking the kind of questions that suggest a diet of quiz shows. How high is it? Can you see France? What happens if you drop a penny? The answers, delivered by a volunteer with the patience of a saint, had the satisfying solidity of facts that have been repeated many times to many generations of curious children. At the top, the wind was even stronger, and the glass was thick and scratched by a century of visitors pressing their faces to it. The sea stretched out in all directions, indifferent and magnificent, and the town below looked like a collection of toys that someone had arranged with love and then forgotten to put away. I stayed longer than was reasonable, just looking, and the volunteer, who had seen this before, said nothing at all, which was exactly right.

There is a temptation, when describing a day like this, to make it sound like a revelation, as if I had returned home a different person, enlightened and serene and ready to throw away my phone and take up weaving. The truth is more modest and, I think, more useful. I came home with wet shoes, a biography of a lighthouse keeper I will probably not finish, and a faint sense of having noticed things. I made tea again, stood at the same window, and watched the light go out of the day in the slow, gradual way that evening light does when nobody is rushing it. The neighbor was unlocking his bicycle again, or perhaps it was a different neighbor, or perhaps it was the same one on a different errand, and I waved, and he waved back, and we neither of us went anywhere in particular. The house settled around me with its familiar creaks and hums. My mind, unaccustomed to idleness, drifted through the day's inventory: the cat on the wall, the sparrow by the bakery, the ladybird on the bench, the dachshund in its coat, the dragon in the bush. It was not a list of achievements. It was a list of witnesses.

Wandering, I have come to think, is not the opposite of purpose. It is a different kind of purpose, one that cannot be measured in outcomes but can be measured in attention. To walk without a destination is to give the world a chance to speak first, to let it offer up its tomatoes in tin cans and its soup of uncertain provenance and its letters that take a week to arrive. It is a small act of trust, the belief that if you are patient and unhurried and slightly curious, something interesting will happen, even if that something is only a fat cat sitting with great seriousness on a wall. In a culture that treats every minute as a resource to be mined, wandering is a form of resistance, not loud or dramatic, but persistent and quietly joyful. It says that a day can be valuable even if nothing was accomplished, that time spent noticing is not time wasted, that the map is not the territory and that sometimes the best route is the one you did not plan to take.

So tomorrow, or perhaps the day after tomorrow, if the rain holds off and the radiator behaves itself, I will do it again. I will leave the phone on the table and walk out without a destination, and I will turn down the lane I have always meant to explore. I will buy a roll I do not need and accept the extra one I did not ask for. I will sit on a bench I have passed a thousand times and watch the ladybird, or its descendant, make its slow progress. I will not be transformed. I will not be suddenly wise. But I will be, for a few hours, exactly where I am, in a particular place, on a particular day, paying attention to the small, unremarkable, entirely sufficient business of being alive in the world. And that, I suspect, is more than enough to be going on with.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I read that somewhere once, underlined it in a library book with a pencil that was not mine, and then spent years trying to understand what it could actually mean in practice. It did not, at first, sound like a description of anything I did. I was busy, distracted, half-present in most rooms, scrolling while people spoke, listening to music while thinking about something else entirely. Generosity suggested giving something away, and I did not feel generous. And yet, slowly, in the unremarkable accumulation of ordinary days, I began to suspect that attention might be less a virtue than a way of seeing, a kind of temperature of the mind. When you truly attend to something, you change its weight. It becomes heavier, more real, more itself.

It begins, most reliably, in the kitchen in the early morning, before the house has decided what kind of day it will be. The light comes in low and sideways, as it does in winter, and finds the dust that the night has settled on everything. It lays itself across the table in a long, pale rectangle, and for a few minutes the chipped mug, the crumbs, the folded newspaper, the small dent in the butter, all of it acquires an importance it has no right to possess. I make tea not because I am thirsty but because the ritual gives my hands something to do while my eyes learn how to be still. The kettle clicks off. Steam rises and vanishes. Somewhere, a pipe knocks. The day has not yet begun to make demands, and in that suspended interval I can practice a kind of attention that asks for nothing.

The chipped mug is blue inside and white outside, and the chip is on the rim where my mouth finds it without thinking, a small irregularity I know by touch. I have owned it for more than a decade, longer than I have owned most things, and it appears in photographs of other people’s birthdays and in the background of video calls, out of focus, faithful. To attend to a mug is a strange ambition, and yet the mug rewards it. There is the faint stain of tea that will never wash out, the way the handle warms my fingers before the tea warms my throat, the slight unevenness of its base that makes it rock if you push it carelessly. Attention turns use into reverence without quite announcing itself as reverence. It simply says: this particular object, in this particular light, at this particular hour, is enough.

Libraries have taught me what that kind of enough can look like when it is institutionalized. I go to the central library not only for books but for the particular silence that lives between the shelves, a silence that is not empty but inhabited. The carpet absorbs sound, the air smells of paper and dust and the faint metal of old radiators, and somewhere a page turns with a soft, papery sigh. I like to walk slowly down the stacks without looking for anything in particular, letting the titles pass like stations. To attend in a library is to accept that you will never read most of what is there, and to find, in that acceptance, a strange relief. The books are not potential; they are presence. They do not need to be finished to be valuable. They wait.

There is a corner on the third floor where the light from a high window falls on a table that no one ever seems to claim for long. Students come and go there, leaving behind pencil shavings and the ghosts of their concentration. I have sat there with notebooks filled with half-sentences and lists that made sense only later, if at all. The dust in that light is visible and purposeful, turning and turning, each mote catching the sun and then losing it. I used to think of dust as dirt, as the sign of neglect. Now I think of it as evidence, a history of all the hands and pages and shoes that have passed through. Attention makes dust interesting. It makes the overlooked into the essential, which may be the whole secret.

Night trains are the other great school of attention I have ever attended. There is something about being carried, in the dark, at speed, through a landscape you cannot properly see, that loosens the tight grip of purpose. The rhythmic clatter steadies the mind. The window becomes a screen on which the world flickers past — a lit farmhouse, a signal glowing red, the brief, intimate brightness of a level crossing, then blackness again. I have crossed countries this way, waking in a berth to find that the language outside the window has changed. You cannot eat quickly on a night train. You cannot text your way through it without feeling the absurdity of the gesture. You sit, and the sitting becomes a kind of thinking.

Strangers on night trains deserve a chapter of their own, because they exist in a suspended category between intimacy and anonymity. The woman opposite me once unfolded an entire picnic from a plastic bag, laying out cheese and bread and an apple with the care of someone setting a table for two, though she was alone. The man in the corridor smoked where he was not supposed to, apologizing to no one, looking out at the passing dark as if it might answer. We shared the small, temporary country of the carriage, its rules and its boredom and its sudden kindnesses, and then, at dawn, we scattered. I remember their hands more clearly than their faces. I remember the way we all, without discussion, leaned toward the window when the sky began to lighten over flat fields, as if light itself were a shared inheritance.

Weather, when you attend to it, is never merely weather. Rain on a train window is a different substance from rain on a tent, which is different again from rain on a city pavement where it splinters on umbrellas and joins the gutters in urgent, silver streams. I have learned to listen for rain the way other people listen for music, to distinguish its intensity by sound alone. A soft rain on leaves is a whispering. A hard rain on a tin roof is a conversation. Indoors, rain turns the windows opaque and the house into a small, well-lit boat. Outdoors, it rearranges the whole geography of the day, making familiar streets into archipelagos, each dry doorway an island. Attention means not complaining about the rain before noticing what it has done to the light.

The garden, if you can call the small, unruly patch behind my house a garden, has been my most patient teacher. It does not respond to my intentions. It responds to season and soil and the occasional, haphazard kindness I show it. In April it is all promise and mud, in June it is a green argument it is having with itself, in September it begins to retreat with a kind of theatrical melancholy. I do not know the names of most of the plants there. I know the dockleaf that will not be evicted, the rose that blooms once, defiantly, in late October, the blackbird that arrives at the same time each evening to inspect the lawn. To attend to a garden is to accept that you are not its author. You are its audience, and occasionally its clumsy assistant.

Music enters the house from upstairs, from a neighbor’s practice that I have overheard for years without ever meeting the person who makes it. Scales in the morning, something more ambitious in the evening, fragments of Sonata, repetitions, sighs. At first I resented it, the way one resents any intrusion into the privacy of one’s thoughts. Then, gradually, I began to listen in the way you listen to weather. The practicing became a timetable, a way of knowing what time it was without a clock. More than that, it became a discipline I could borrow. The slow scales are an exercise in attention itself: the same notes, again and again, with only the smallest improvements in tone and touch. That is not failure. That is the work.

I have tried to listen to music the way that neighbor practices it, which is to say, completely and without multitasking. It is harder than it sounds. A song will begin and my mind will immediately furnish it with memories, with errands, with a conversation I had three years ago that I am suddenly, urgently, revising. To listen without those intrusions requires a kind of muscular self-denial. And yet, when I manage it, even for a few minutes, the music changes from background to foreground, from decoration to event. A chord resolves and something in my chest resolves with it. I understand, in the body, why people have always considered listening a sacred act.

Letters are attention made portable. I keep a box of them, tied with string that is too short, in the bottom of a wardrobe, and I take it down rarely and always with a certain ceremony, as if I were visiting someone. There are letters from my mother written when she was young and daring, full of exclamation marks and reports of dances I cannot picture her attending. There are letters from friends who have moved away and now communicate in the brief, efficient pulses of the present. To read a letter is to enter a mind at a slower speed than thought allows. The writer chose words, crossed them out, began again. The ink has faded where the sun touched it. Attention, here, becomes an act of rescue.

One letter, in particular, has survived every move I have made since I was eighteen. It is not important in content. It describes a train journey, a bad hotel, a misunderstanding about a ferry, but it is written in a hand I know better than my own, and it cracks me open every time I read the opening line, which is simply: “I have been thinking about the light in the kitchen.” The writer was my grandmother, who died in the house where that light still falls each morning. She was describing, decades before me, the very table I now sit at. Attention, it turns out, can be hereditary. We learn to notice from those who noticed before us, even if we never say so aloud.

Cities complicate attention because they compete for it so aggressively. Every surface shouts, every screen glows, every window promises a product or a person I do not need. The market near my flat is an exception, and I go there not to buy anything in particular, though I always buy something, but to practice a different kind of noticing. The fishmonger calls out the names of fish as if they were old friends. The flower seller arranges and rearranges her buckets with a sculptor’s concentration. Children are dragged, reluctantly, past the cheese stall. To attend in a city is to choose, endlessly, what to let in and what to let pass, and to accept that the choice itself is exhausting and human.

The sea does not require choosing. It overwhelms choosing. I grew up near the coast, close enough to smell salt on windy days, and I return whenever I can, not for swimming, though I swim, but for the sheer, undifferentiated vastness of it. The sea is attention on a planetary scale. It has been noticing the shore, in its way, for millions of years, worrying at rocks, lifting and dropping pebbles, leaving and returning. On a clear day, the horizon is so clean it seems drawn. On a rough day, the waves arrive with an insistence that rearranges your priorities. You stand there, windburned and damp, and feel, absurdly, both tiny and included.

Night skies do the same work more quietly. I drive out, sometimes, when the moon is new and the clouds are thin, to places where the streetlights end and the stars begin to assert themselves. It takes time for the eyes to adjust, and longer for the mind to accept that the faint smudge overhead is not a smudge at all but a galaxy, and that the darker patches between the stars are not emptiness but dust. Attention, at night, is a matter of patience. You cannot rush into seeing. You wait, and the sky, which has waited for you, slowly reveals itself. There is a parable in that for almost everything else.

Work, when it is done with the hands, is attention embodied. I am not a maker by trade, but I have spent enough time in workshops and kitchens and sheds to know the particular silence that falls when someone is really doing a task. The carpenter listening to wood. The cook tasting, adjusting, tasting again. The seamstress threading a needle for the third time without irritation. Hands teach the mind what attention feels like: not as a grand spiritual state but as a steady, repeatable application of care. You sand, you check, you sand again. The surface improves by increments too small to see. That is not inefficiency. That is the whole point.

My grandmother’s hands are my standard for this. She could shell peas, mend a shirt, knead dough, and do all of it while carrying on a conversation that required her full intelligence. Her attention was not divided; it was layered, like music with a bass line. She noticed the weather in her knees, the mood of the room in the pause before an answer, the exact moment tea was ready by the sound of the pot. I did not inherit her skill, but I inherited the aspiration. When I am at my best, I am trying, however clumsily, to do several necessary things at once without dropping any of them, and to know, without thinking, which one needs me most.

Photographs were once meant to preserve attention, to fix a moment so it could be returned to. Now they mostly proliferate, taken and never looked at, stored in clouds that evaporate when the subscription lapses. I have a shoebox of printed photographs, the kind with white borders, and it is my favorite archive. I look at it rarely, but when I do, I am struck by how much attention is visible in the images themselves. A photograph of a birthday cake, slightly blurred, because the photographer was laughing.
